lessons.title: From PL-900 to AB-410
lessons.summaryHtml:
AB-410: Building Intelligent Applications is the associate exam for people who build business solutions on Power Platform with Copilot, prompts and low-code tools. It replaced PL-200, which retired on 31 August 2026, and passing it earns Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate.

  • PL-900 asked what each tool does. AB-410 asks you to choose, configure and connect them for a real scenario.
  • Three areas: foundation for intelligent applications (25–30%), intelligent applications (25–30%) and business logic and automation (40–45%).
  • You work in a developer environment, keep everything in the Campus Help Desk solution (prefix chd) and test it in a second environment.

The exam lasts 120 minutes and you need 700 to pass. The certification renews every year with a free online assessment.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

AB-410: Building Intelligent Applications is the associate exam for people who build business solutions on Power Platform. It checks that you can take a real requirement and turn it into Dataverse tables, model-driven and canvas apps, cloud flows, AI prompts and agents that work together.

Think of PL-900 as learning the names of every tool in a workshop. AB-410 is the day the instructor hands you a job card and watches you build the cupboard. You must pick the right tool, set it up correctly and explain why you chose it.

Passing AB-410 earns Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate. The exam lasts 120 minutes and the passing score is 700. Like other associate certifications, it stays valid for a year, and you renew it with a free online assessment on Microsoft Learn.

Why it matters

Companies no longer want apps that only store data. They want apps that summarise long records, classify requests, suggest next steps and hand work to agents. AB-410 was written for that world. It tests whether you can add AI in the right place, with the right controls, and still build a clean data model underneath.

For you, it is the natural next step after PL-900. It proves you can deliver a working solution, not just describe one. It is also the base for the developer track (AB-400) if you later move into code.

How it works

1. How AB-410 differs from PL-900 and PL-200.

PL-900PL-200 (retired)AB-410
LevelFundamentalsAssociateAssociate
Main questionWhat does this tool do?How does a functional consultant configure the platform?How do you build an intelligent solution for this scenario?
StatusCurrentRetired on 31 August 2026Current; replaced PL-200
AI focusAwareness of Copilot and agentsLighterCentral: prompt columns, row summaries, generative pages, AI Hub prompts and models, agents from apps

Many PL-200 skills carry over: Dataverse tables and security, model-driven and canvas apps, cloud flows, business rules and business process flows. What changes is the emphasis. AB-410 expects you to design with AI-enabled tools such as Plan designer, and to use prompts and AI models inside apps and flows.

2. The three exam areas.

AreaWeightWhat it covers
Create a foundation for intelligent applications25–30%Design with AI-enabled tools, built-in agents, extensibility, environment types, solutions and ALM; data models including tables, columns, relationships, prompt columns, row summaries, views, main forms and security
Create intelligent applications25–30%Model-driven apps (forms, views, generative pages, app access, charts, dashboards) and canvas apps (data, accessibility, performance, components, variables, error handling, testing, agents from a canvas app)
Build business application logic and automation40–45%Cloud flows, approvals and troubleshooting; AI Hub prompts and AI models in apps and flows; business rules, business process flows, and calculated, rollup and formula columns
Remember: the third area is the biggest. Nearly half your score comes from logic and automation, so give it the most lab time.

3. Prerequisites. Microsoft expects you to arrive with:

  • Familiarity with Copilot in Power Apps, Power Automate, Power Pages and Dataverse.
  • Awareness of how agents are created in Copilot Studio.
  • Basic knowledge of AI models and prompts in AI Hub.
  • The ability to map a business process to a flow, an agent or an app feature.
  • Working knowledge of Dataverse and Power Fx, the formula language of canvas apps.
  • Awareness of environment governance, security roles, data policies and the solution lifecycle.

PL-900 gave you the vocabulary for all of these. This track fills in the depth.

4. Your environments. An environment is a separate space with its own Dataverse database, apps and flows. Real teams never build in production. You will copy that habit.

EnvironmentTypePurpose
CHD DevDeveloperWhere you build. The solution here is unmanaged, so you can edit everything.
CHD TestDeveloperWhere you import the managed solution and check it works like a real user would see it.

You create both with the free Power Apps Developer Plan. A developer environment is meant for one person to build and learn in. In a company, test would usually be a sandbox environment, but two developer environments teach the same idea.

5. The Campus Help Desk solution. A solution is a box that holds your components so they move together. Its publisher supplies the prefix chd, so your columns get schema names such as chd_priority and chd_duedate. You set the solution as the preferred solution, so anything you create in CHD Dev lands in it automatically.

6. Study approach.

  1. Print or copy the official skills list and tick each bullet as you complete it.
  2. For each lesson, read, do the lab in CHD Dev, then answer the quiz without notes.
  3. Every few lessons, export a managed solution and import it into CHD Test. This builds real ALM muscle memory.
  4. Practise explaining choices aloud: "I used a business rule because the logic is simple and must run on the form and on the server."
  5. Use the free practice assessment on Microsoft Learn near the end, and revisit the areas where you score lowest.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Here is how the running project grows in this track.

  1. Foundation. You keep Ticket and Category and extend Ticket with columns such as Ticket Number (autonumber), Channel and Resolved On. You reuse the standard Contact table for students. You add a prompt column that summarises long ticket descriptions and turn on row summaries.
  2. Apps. The Help Desk Staff model-driven app gets better forms and views, a generative page for a triage board, and a dashboard. The student canvas app gets reusable components, error handling and an agent built from the app.
  3. Logic. You add a business process flow with stages New, Assigned, Resolved and Closed. You create an AI Hub prompt that classifies each new ticket into a category and call it from a cloud flow. Business rules and formula columns handle simple rules such as "overdue".
  4. ALM. Everything lives in the Campus Help Desk solution with prefix chd. You export it as managed and import it into CHD Test after each milestone.

Common mistakes

  • Studying AB-410 like PL-900, by memorising definitions. The exam gives scenarios and asks which option fits best.
  • Building outside a solution. Components created in the Default Solution with a random prefix are hard to move later.
  • Skipping the logic and automation labs because apps feel more fun. That area carries the most weight.
  • Assuming PL-200 notes are enough. Newer topics such as prompt columns, row summaries, generative pages and AI Hub prompts are central now.
  • Testing only as the maker. You must also check what a user with a limited security role sees.

How the exam asks about it

  • Most questions describe a business need and several possible components. Clue words such as "without code", "summarise", "classify" or "guide users through stages" point to specific features you will meet in later lessons.
  • Expect "choose the best option" questions where two answers work but one is simpler, cheaper or more secure. Pick the one that meets every stated requirement with the least effort.
  • ALM appears across topics: "move to production", "different values per environment" or "prevent changes in test" all point back to solutions, environment variables and managed solutions.

quiz.question: A colleague passed PL-200 in 2025 and asks what replaced it after its retirement. Which exam and credential should you point them to?
options: AB-410 and Intelligent Applications Builder Associate
AB-400 and Power Platform Developer Associate
quiz.explanation: AB-410 replaced PL-200, which retired on 31 August 2026. Passing it earns Microsoft Certified: Intelligent Applications Builder Associate.

quiz.question: You have two weeks left before your AB-410 exam and limited time. Based on the skill weights, which area should get the most practice?
quiz.explanation: Build business application logic and automation is 40–45% of the exam, the largest area. It covers cloud flows, AI Hub prompts and models, and business logic.

quiz.question: You want to learn AB-410 without affecting your college’s shared default environment. You also want a separate place to test managed solutions. What should you set up?
options: Two developer environments: one to build, one to test
Build in the default environment and test in a Teams environment
One trial environment for both building and testing
A single production environment with two solutions
quiz.explanation: The Developer Plan gives you personal developer environments. Building in one and importing managed solutions into another mirrors a real dev and test setup.

quiz.question: You create a new table in your solution, but its schema name starts with cr8a1_ instead of chd_. What is the most likely cause?
options: The table was created as an elastic table
Auditing is turned off for the environment
The environment has no Dataverse database
The solution uses a different publisher than your Campus Help Desk publisher
quiz.explanation: The prefix comes from the solution’s publisher. A default publisher gives a random-looking prefix; a solution tied to the chd publisher gives chd_.

lessons.title: Design solutions with AI-enabled tools
lessons.summaryHtml:
Before you build, you design. AB-410 expects you to read a set of requirements and pick the right Power Platform components, often with help from AI tools such as Plan designer and Copilot.

  • Analyze requirements: map each need to a table, app, flow, agent, prompt or site.
  • Evaluate built-in agents: Copilot chat in model-driven apps, form fill assistance, row summaries and autonomous agents shown in the agent feed.
  • Recommend extensibility when low-code is not enough: custom connectors, PCF components, plug-ins, code apps or Azure services.
  • Recommend environment types: developer, sandbox, production, trial, default and Dataverse for Teams.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Designing a solution means deciding what to build before you build it. You read the requirements, split them into small needs, and match each need to a Power Platform part: a table, an app, a flow, a prompt, an agent or a site.

It is like an architect planning a house. Before anyone lays a brick, the architect decides where the kitchen, stairs and windows go. A mistake on paper costs minutes. A mistake in concrete costs weeks.

AB-410 adds a twist: you design with AI-enabled tools. Copilot can draft a plan, suggest tables and even propose which agents to use. Your job is to judge that draft and fix it.

Why it matters

Most failed projects fail at design, not at build. Someone builds a canvas app when staff needed a model-driven app. Someone writes a plug-in when a business rule was enough. Someone builds everything in the default environment and then cannot move it.

Good design saves licences, time and support effort. It also keeps AI features where they help, such as summarising a long ticket, and away from places where a simple rule is safer and cheaper.

How it works

1. Analyze requirements. Turn each sentence of the brief into a need, then into a component. Ask who uses it, on what device, how much data, and whether it must run without a person.

Requirement clueLikely component
Structured data, relationships, security by teamDataverse tables
Staff work with many related records, views and formsModel-driven app
Custom, mobile-friendly screens for a specific taskCanvas app
Something must happen when a row changes, on a schedule or on emailCloud flow
Summarise, classify, extract or draft textAI Hub prompt, prompt column or row summary
Answer questions in chat or act on its ownCopilot Studio agent
External users, such as the public, need a websitePower Pages

2. Use AI-enabled design tools. Plan designer lets you describe a business problem in plain language, optionally with documents or images. Copilot drafts a plan with roles, user stories, a process map, a Dataverse data model and suggested apps, flows and agents. You review and edit the plan, then generate components from it. Copilot can also create tables from a description. Treat every AI draft as a first version that needs your review.

3. Evaluate built-in agents and AI features. Before building something new, check what already exists.

  • Copilot chat in model-driven apps: users ask questions about their data in a side pane.
  • Form fill assistance and smart paste: help users complete forms faster.
  • Row summaries: AI-generated summaries of a record on forms and views.
  • Autonomous agents in the agent feed: agents built in Copilot Studio can log work for review, and the model-driven app shows it in the agent feed. You add an agent to the feed from the app designer’s Agents area.
  • Copilot Studio agents: for chat experiences in Teams, a website or an app.

Most of these must be enabled by an admin for the tenant and environment, and some need the modern look for model-driven apps.

4. Recommend extensibility. When low-code cannot meet a requirement, you recommend, not build, a code option. The AB-400 developer track builds them.

NeedExtensibility option
Call an API that has no connectorCustom connector
A custom control on a form, such as a star ratingPCF code component
Server-side logic that must run in the same transaction as a savePlug-in
A fully custom web front end, such as a React dashboardCode app
Long-running or heavy processing outside DataverseAzure Functions or other Azure services

5. Recommend environment types.

TypeBest forKey trait
DeveloperOne person learning or buildingCreated with the Developer Plan; personal
SandboxTeam development and testingNon-production; supports copy and reset
ProductionLive business usePermanent, backed up, fully governed
TrialShort evaluationsCleaned up after 30 days
DefaultPersonal productivity appsOne per tenant, shared by all licensed users, cannot be deleted
Dataverse for TeamsSimple apps inside a Teams teamCreated from Teams; limited admin control
Watch out: the default environment is not a good home for business solutions. Everyone with a licence can make things there, so it is hard to govern.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The brief says: students report issues on their phones; staff triage and resolve them; managers want weekly numbers; long descriptions slow staff down; some tickets arrive by email.
  2. You open Plan designer and paste the brief. It proposes Ticket, Category and a student table, a canvas app, a model-driven app and a flow.
  3. You review the plan. You replace the new student table with the standard Contact table. You keep Ticket and Category.
  4. You map the rest: phone screens go to the canvas app; triage goes to the Help Desk Staff model-driven app; email tickets go to a cloud flow with the Outlook "When a new email arrives" trigger; long descriptions go to a prompt column and row summaries; weekly numbers go to a model-driven dashboard.
  5. You evaluate built-in agents. Copilot chat in the model-driven app can answer "how many High tickets are open?" without building anything. An autonomous triage agent could log suggested categories to the agent feed for staff to confirm.
  6. One need remains: look up student details from the university’s Campus Directory API. No connector exists, so you recommend a custom connector.
  7. You recommend a developer environment to build, a sandbox to test and a production environment to go live.

Common mistakes

  • Accepting the Plan designer output without review. It is a draft; check tables against existing standard tables.
  • Jumping to code. A plug-in or PCF control is not the answer if a business rule or a built-in control works.
  • Building a new AI feature when a built-in one, such as row summaries or Copilot chat, already meets the need.
  • Choosing a trial environment for anything that must last beyond a month.
  • Forgetting that AI features need admin enablement in the environment.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Describe the process in natural language and get a draft data model and components" points to Plan designer.
  • "Reset", "copy" or "test without affecting production" points to a sandbox. "Single maker learning" points to a developer environment.
  • "No connector exists for the API" points to a custom connector. "Custom visual control on a form" points to a PCF component.
  • "Review what an agent did" or "human in the loop inside the app" points to the agent feed.

terms.definition: A Copilot experience where you describe a business problem and get a draft plan: roles, user stories, a process map, a data model and suggested apps, flows and agents.
An AI capability that already exists in the product, such as Copilot chat in a model-driven app, that you enable and configure instead of building.
A pane in a model-driven app that shows what autonomous agents did and what they need a person to review.
Adding code-based parts, such as a PCF control or a plug-in, when out-of-the-box features cannot meet a requirement.
A non-production environment for development and testing that supports copy and reset.

lessons.examTip: Always check for a built-in or low-code option first. The exam rewards the simplest option that fully meets the requirement.

steps: Download the exercise files and read requirements-brief.md from top to bottom.
In CHD Dev, open Plan designer and paste the Background and Roles sections of requirements-brief.md as your description.
Review the generated plan: roles, user stories, process map and suggested tables. Compare the tables with your Ticket and Category tables and staff.csv.
Go through R1 to R12 in the brief and note which ones the plan covered. Write at least three it missed at the top of decision-table-template.md.
Open Help Desk Staff in the app designer and review the Copilot and agent settings. Note which built-in AI features could meet R5 and R6.
Fill every row of decision-table-template.md with a component, a reason and any extensibility, then fill the environment-type table.
Compare your answers with the model answer at the bottom of the file and mark any row where your choice differs, with a reason.
check: Your decision table has 12 rows, R1 to R12, with no empty Component cells.
Exactly one requirement, R12 (the asset system REST API), needs extensibility: a custom connector.
R9 (visitors without an account) maps to Power Pages and R8 (chat at any hour) to a Copilot Studio agent.
R7 and R11 map to scheduled cloud flows, and R4 maps to an automated cloud flow triggered by email.
Your environment table lists Developer for development, Sandbox for test and Production for live use.

quiz.question: Help desk staff want to see, inside their model-driven app, which tickets an autonomous agent has triaged and which ones need a human to confirm. What should you recommend?
options: A Power BI dashboard embedded in the form
Add the agent to the app’s agent feed
A canvas app with a gallery of agent logs
A business process flow stage called Agent
quiz.explanation: The agent feed in model-driven apps shows agent activity and items waiting for human review. Autonomous agents are added to the feed from the app designer.

quiz.question: A team needs a place to test a solution before production. They want to reset it to a clean state between test cycles. Which environment type fits best?
quiz.explanation: Sandbox environments are non-production and support copy and reset. The default environment is shared and cannot be reset; trials expire.

quiz.question: The help desk must read student details from a university REST API that has no existing Power Platform connector. Apps and flows both need it. What do you recommend?
quiz.explanation: A custom connector wraps a REST API so canvas apps, flows and agents can call it. It is the standard extensibility option when no connector exists.

quiz.question: A manager describes the whole help desk process in two paragraphs and wants a first draft of tables, apps, flows and agents to review with you. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: Plan designer takes a natural-language description, and optionally documents or images, and drafts a plan with requirements, a data model and suggested components that you review before generating.

lessons.title: Solutions and ALM strategy
lessons.summaryHtml:
Application lifecycle management (ALM) is how a solution moves safely from development to test to production. In Power Platform, the unit you move is a solution.

  • Build in an unmanaged solution in development. Deploy a managed solution to test and production.
  • Every solution has a publisher; its prefix (here chd) goes on every schema name.
  • Environment variables and connection references hold the values that change per environment, so you never edit a flow after import.
  • Solution layers explain which change wins. Pipelines in Power Platform automate deployment between environments.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Application lifecycle management, or ALM, is the set of habits that move your work safely from "being built" to "being used". In Power Platform, the thing you move is a solution.

Think of a restaurant. The chef tests a new dish in the test kitchen, a few staff taste it, and only then does it go on the menu. Nobody experiments on a customer’s plate. Development, test and production environments are the test kitchen, the tasting table and the dining room.

Why it matters

Without ALM, makers edit apps directly in production. A small change breaks a flow at 9 a.m. on exam results day. Nobody knows what changed, and nobody can roll it back.

With ALM, every change is built in development, packaged in a solution, tested, and then deployed. Settings that differ per environment, such as email addresses and connections, are kept outside the logic, so nothing needs hand editing after deployment.

How it works

1. Publishers and prefixes. Every solution belongs to a publisher. The publisher’s prefix, chd in our case, is added to every schema name, such as chd_ticket. Choice values also get a numeric prefix from the publisher. Use one publisher for your organisation or project and create it before you build anything, because the prefix is fixed once a component is created.

2. Managed and unmanaged.

UnmanagedManaged
WhereDevelopmentTest and production
Can you edit components?YesNot directly, unless the component allows customisation through managed properties
Removing the solutionRemoves only the container; components stayRemoves the components and their data
PurposeThe source you work inThe package you deploy

3. Solution layers. A component can be changed by several solutions. Dataverse stacks the changes as layers. Managed layers sit at the bottom in install order. The unmanaged Active layer sits on top. The top layer wins. If someone edits a form directly in production, that unmanaged change sits above your managed layer and hides your later updates. You can see this with Solution layers on the component and remove the active customisation.

4. Environment variables and connection references.

  • An environment variable stores a setting such as text, a number, a yes/no value, JSON, a data source or a secret held in Azure Key Vault. It has a default value and a current value. You supply the current value per environment, often during import.
  • A connection reference lets a flow or app use a connector without being tied to one person’s connection. During import, you pick or create the connection for that environment.
Remember: values change per environment, so keep them outside the logic. The flow reads the variable; the variable’s value changes; the flow never changes.

5. Solution strategy. Keep all project components in one solution when the project is small, like Campus Help Desk. Larger projects sometimes split into several solutions, such as a data model solution and an apps solution, but that adds dependencies: one solution needs another installed first. Set your solution as the preferred solution so new components land in it. Avoid building in the Default Solution. Run Solution checker before export to catch issues.

6. Moving solutions.

ApproachWhen
Manual export and importLearning, very small teams
Pipelines in Power PlatformMakers want a simple in-product deployment from dev to test to production
Source control (Git) integrationTeams want solution files versioned in a Git repository
Build Tools with Azure DevOps or GitHub ActionsProfessional CI/CD with automated checks

When you import a newer version of a managed solution, you can upgrade it, which also removes components you deleted in development.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. In CHD Dev, the solution Campus Help Desk uses the publisher with prefix chd.
  2. The "New ticket alert" flow emailed a fixed address. You create an environment variable Support Email (schema name chd_SupportEmail) and use it as the flow’s To value.
  3. The flow already uses connection references for Dataverse and Office 365 Outlook, because it was created inside the solution.
  4. You run Solution checker, then export as managed. With the pac CLI the export looks like this: 
    pac auth create --environment https://chd-dev.crm.dynamics.com
pac solution export --name CampusHelpDesk --path ./CampusHelpDesk_managed.zip --managed
    Your environment URL will differ.
  5. You import into CHD Test. The import asks for the Support Email value and the connections. You enter a test mailbox.
  6. Later, a tester edits a Ticket view directly in CHD Test. Your next import does not seem to change it. You open Solution layers, see the unmanaged Active layer, and remove the active customisation.

Common mistakes

  • Building with the default publisher and ending up with a random prefix on every column.
  • Importing unmanaged solutions into production, which lets anyone edit components there.
  • Hard-coding URLs, emails or IDs in flows instead of using environment variables.
  • Making "quick fixes" directly in test or production, which creates an unmanaged layer that hides future updates.
  • Deleting an unmanaged solution and expecting its components to disappear. They stay in the environment.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Prevent changes in production" or "deploy to downstream environments" points to managed solutions.
  • "Value differs per environment" points to an environment variable. "Each environment uses its own account or connection" points to a connection reference.
  • "Change is not visible after import" or "which customisation is applied" points to solution layers.
  • "Simple, built-in deployment for makers" points to Pipelines in Power Platform; "Azure DevOps" or "GitHub Actions" points to Build Tools.

terms.definition: A locked, packaged solution for deployment. Its components cannot be edited directly in the target, and uninstalling it removes them.
An editable solution used during development. It is the source you work in and export from.
A solution component that stores a setting, such as an email address or URL, whose value can differ in each environment.
A solution component that points a flow or app to a connection, so each environment can supply its own connection.
One level in the stack of changes to a component. The top layer, often the unmanaged Active layer, is what users see.
A built-in feature that deploys solutions from a development environment through test to production.

lessons.examTip: “Different value in test and production without editing the flow” means environment variable. “Different connection per environment” means connection reference.

steps: Download the exercise files and open environment-values.md.
In the Campus Help Desk solution in CHD Dev, create the environment variable Support Email (schema chd_SupportEmail, Text) with the CHD Dev current value from environment-values.md.
Open the new-ticket notification flow and replace the hard-coded To address in Send an email (V2) with Support Email from dynamic content. Save.
Open Connection references in the solution and check that the flow uses one for Microsoft Dataverse and one for Office 365 Outlook, as listed in environment-values.md.
Run Solution checker on the solution and read any warnings.
Export the solution as managed and import it into CHD Test. When prompted, enter helpdesk-test@staff.example.edu (or your second address) and pick a connection for each reference.
In CHD Test, create the test ticket from environment-values.md and check which mailbox receives the email.
Open the Ticket table in CHD Test, select a column and open Solution layers.
Optional: run the commands in pac-commands.txt, then compare the generated deploy-settings.json with the sample file.
check: In CHD Dev the flow’s To field shows the Support Email variable, not a typed address.
In CHD Test, Support Email shows the test value, and the email for "Deployment test: projector in Hall B" arrives at that address, not the Dev one.
The solution contains exactly 2 connection references: Dataverse and Office 365 Outlook.
Solution layers in CHD Test shows a managed layer from Campus Help Desk.
If you used pac, the generated settings file has one EnvironmentVariables entry (chd_SupportEmail) and two ConnectionReferences entries.

quiz.question: After importing the Campus Help Desk solution into production, flows still email the developer’s test mailbox. You want each environment to use its own support address without editing the flow. What should you use?
quiz.explanation: An environment variable stores a value that can differ per environment. You set the production value during or after import; the flow reads it.

quiz.question: Your organization wants test and production to be locked so that nobody changes components there directly. What should you deploy?
options: A copy of the development environment
quiz.explanation: Managed solutions are the recommended format for downstream environments. They prevent direct editing and can be cleanly upgraded or removed.

quiz.question: A column label in production shows a value that is not in your latest managed solution. Someone edited it directly in production. Where do you look to understand this?
quiz.explanation: Solution layers show every layer applied to a component. An unmanaged Active layer on top overrides your managed layer until it is removed.

quiz.question: A small team wants a simple, built-in way to move solutions from development to test to production with approvals, without building Azure DevOps pipelines. What do you recommend?
options: A cloud flow that copies tables
quiz.explanation: Pipelines in Power Platform give makers an in-product deployment process between environments. Build Tools and Azure DevOps are for more advanced CI/CD.

lessons.title: Tables and columns in depth
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dataverse tables are the foundation of every Campus Help Desk app. At associate level you choose the right table type, ownership and properties, and the right column type and behaviour for each piece of data.

  • Create tables from blank, with Copilot, by importing Excel, CSV or a SharePoint list, or visually in the data workspace.
  • Standard tables such as Contact and Account already exist. Extend them before you build a duplicate.
  • Ownership (user or team, or organization) is set at creation and cannot be changed later.
  • Column choices include choice versus choices, date behaviours, autonumber, file and image, and formula columns.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A Dataverse table is like a well-designed form that everyone fills in the same way. Each column is one question on that form, with rules about what kind of answer is allowed.

In PL-900 you created Ticket and Category. At associate level you make sharper choices: which kind of table, who owns its rows, which properties to switch on, and exactly which column type and behaviour fits each piece of data.

Why it matters

Table decisions are hard to undo. Ownership cannot change after creation. A column’s data type cannot simply be switched later. A wrong choice can block security, break reporting, or force you to rebuild and migrate data.

Good choices make everything above them easier. Views filter correctly, security works by team, AI features such as prompt columns and row summaries have clean data to work with, and flows can rely on consistent values.

How it works

1. Ways to create tables.

  • New table with properties you set yourself.
  • Start with Copilot: describe the data and Copilot proposes tables, columns and relationships for you to review.
  • Import from an Excel or CSV file or a SharePoint list. AI helps map the columns.
  • The data workspace: a visual designer where you create tables and relationships on a diagram and see the whole model. It does not support every column type, so some columns are added later in the table designer.
  • Virtual tables that show external data without copying it into Dataverse.

2. Table types and ownership.

ChoiceOptionsWhen
TypeStandard, Activity, Virtual, ElasticStandard for most business data; Activity for things with a date and time like calls or tasks; Virtual for external data; Elastic for very high volumes
OwnershipUser or team, OrganizationUser or team when access depends on who owns a row; Organization for shared reference data such as Category
Watch out: ownership and the schema name are fixed once the table is saved. Decide them before you click Save.

3. Standard tables. Dataverse ships with tables such as Contact, Account and User. Other apps and built-in features already understand them. Extend them with your own columns, for example a Student ID on Contact, before you create a duplicate table.

4. Table properties. Useful ones include:

  • Primary column: the name shown in lookups, such as Title for Ticket.
  • Enable attachments: lets users add notes and files.
  • Audit changes: records who changed what. Auditing must also be on for the environment.
  • Track changes: supports data synchronisation.
  • Can be taken offline, Appear in search results, and duplicate detection.

5. Column types.

TypeUseHelp Desk example
Single line of text (with formats such as Email, Phone, URL)Short textTitle, Room
Multiple lines of textLong textDescription, Resolution Notes
Whole number, Decimal, Float, CurrencyNumbers and moneySatisfaction score, Repair cost
Choice / ChoicesOne / many values from a fixed listPriority / Affected services
Yes/NoTwo optionsNeeds on-site visit
Date only, Date and timeDatesDue Date, Resolved On
LookupLink to a row in another tableCategory, Student (Contact)
AutonumberReadable sequential IDCHD-1001
File, ImageStored files and picturesScreenshot of the error
FormulaValue calculated with Power FxIs Overdue
PromptValue generated by an AI promptDescription summary (lesson A.6)

6. Important column settings.

  • Required: Optional, Business recommended or Business required.
  • Local or global choice: a global choice is defined once and reused on many tables, so the options stay in sync.
  • Date behaviour: User local converts to each user’s time zone; Date only stores a calendar date with no conversion; Time zone independent stores the date and time exactly as entered. You can change User local to one of the others, but not back.
  • Searchable and column security: control whether a column appears in search and who can read or update it.

A formula column is written in Power Fx and calculated when the row is read, so it is always current. For example, a Yes/No formula could combine Due Date and Status to show whether a ticket is overdue. You will build formula, calculated and rollup columns in lesson A.17.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Ticket is user or team owned, so staff can later see only their team’s tickets. Category is organization owned, because it is shared reference data.
  2. You add Ticket Number (chd_ticketnumber) as an Autonumber column with the prefix CHD- so staff can quote a readable ID on the phone.
  3. You add Channel as a choice column synced with a global choice chd_channel (Web, Email, Walk-in). A future Feedback table can reuse it.
  4. You add Resolved On as Date only, because "resolved on 12 March" must look the same for every user, and Resolution Notes as multiple lines of text.
  5. You add Screenshot as an Image column and turn on Audit changes for Ticket.
  6. Instead of a new Student table, you add Student ID to the standard Contact table and create a lookup on Ticket called Reported By that points to Contact.
  7. You open the data workspace to see Ticket, Category and Contact on one diagram and check the lookups.

Common mistakes

  • Creating a table as organization owned and later needing row security by owner or team. Ownership cannot be changed.
  • Using a text column for values that should come from a fixed list. Choice columns keep data clean for views, charts and flows.
  • Leaving a birthday or due date as User local, so it shifts by a day for users in other time zones.
  • Creating duplicate tables for people or organisations instead of extending Contact and Account.
  • Turning on auditing for the table but not for the environment, then wondering why nothing is recorded.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Access based on the owner or team" points to user or team ownership. "Shared lookup data everyone reads" points to organization ownership.
  • "Same date for all users regardless of time zone" points to Date only. "Store the exact local time entered" points to Time zone independent.
  • "Select more than one value" points to choices. "Reuse the same list on several tables" points to a global choice.
  • "Readable, incrementing reference number" points to autonumber. "Build tables visually and see relationships" points to the data workspace.

quiz.explanation: Reusing and extending standard tables keeps data in one place and works with built-in features. Create a new table only when a standard one does not fit.

lessons.title: Relationships, views and main forms
lessons.summaryHtml:
Relationships connect Dataverse tables. A one-to-many relationship adds a lookup column on the "many" table; a many-to-many relationship uses an intersect table. Each one-to-many relationship also has a behavior that decides what happens to child rows when you delete, assign, share or reparent the parent.

  • Parental: actions on the parent cascade to all children. Referential, Remove Link: deleting the parent just clears the lookup. Referential, Restrict Delete: the parent cannot be deleted while children exist. Custom: you choose per action.
  • Public views are shared lists of rows with chosen columns, filters and sort order. Each table also has system views such as Quick Find and Lookup.
  • Main forms are built from tabs, sections, columns and components such as subgrids and quick view controls.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse tables rarely stand alone. A ticket belongs to a category. A ticket has many comments. A staff member can follow many tickets, and a ticket can have many followers. Relationships describe these links. Views are saved lists of rows. Main forms are the screens where users read and edit one row.

Think of a family tree and a phone book. The family tree is the relationship: it says who belongs to whom. The phone book page is a view: a filtered, sorted list. A person’s full profile card is the form.

At PL-900 level you learned that relationships exist. At AB-410 level you must also decide how they behave: what happens to the children when the parent is deleted, reassigned or shared.

Why it matters

Picture a help desk where a staff member deletes the Category “Wi-Fi”. What should happen to the 300 tickets that use it? Delete them all? Keep them with an empty category? Block the delete? Each answer is correct for some business, and wrong for another.

The same is true for ownership. If a ticket moves to another agent, should its comments move too? If they do not, the new owner may not even be able to read them. Relationship behavior answers these questions once, at the data level, so every app, flow and API call follows the same rule.

How it works

1. Relationship types.

TypeWhat is createdHelp Desk example
One-to-many (1:N) / many-to-one (N:1)A lookup column on the "many" table. It is the same relationship seen from each side.One Category has many Tickets; Ticket has a Category lookup.
Many-to-many (N:N), nativeA hidden intersect table that only stores pairs of row IDs.Categories and the staff who are experts in them.
Many-to-many, manual (custom intersect table)Your own table with two N:1 lookups. It can hold extra columns.Ticket Follower with Ticket, Staff, Date added and Role.
Self-referentialA lookup from a table to itself.Ticket has a Parent ticket lookup for duplicates.

2. Relationship behavior. Every 1:N relationship has a behavior. It controls what happens to the child rows (the "referencing" rows) when an action happens on the parent row. In the maker portal you choose one of four behavior types under the relationship’s advanced options.

BehaviorEffectWhen to use
Referential, Remove LinkYou can navigate between rows, but actions on the parent do not affect the children. Deleting the parent clears the lookup on the children.Loose links, such as Ticket to Category when orphaned tickets are acceptable.
Referential, Restrict DeleteSame as referential, but the parent cannot be deleted while children exist.Reference data that must stay, such as Category.
ParentalEvery action on the parent is also applied to all children.Children that cannot exist without the parent, such as Ticket Comments.
CustomYou pick the behavior for each action yourself.Mixed needs, such as cascade Assign but restrict Delete.

3. Actions and cascade options. With Custom behavior you set each action separately.

ActionOptions
Assign (change owner)Cascade All, Cascade Active, Cascade User-Owned, Cascade None
Share / UnshareCascade All, Cascade Active, Cascade User-Owned, Cascade None
Reparent (the lookup changes to a new parent)Cascade All, Cascade Active, Cascade User-Owned, Cascade None
DeleteCascade All, Remove Link, Restrict
MergeCascade All, Cascade None
  • Cascade All: apply the action to every related child row.
  • Cascade Active: only children whose state is Active.
  • Cascade User-Owned: only children owned by the same user as the parent.
  • Cascade None: do nothing to the children.
  • Reparent is about inherited access. When a child moves under a new parent, the owner of the new parent can gain access to it.
Watch out: a cascading Assign on a parent with thousands of children can take time and touches every child row. Choose Cascade Active or User-Owned when you only need part of the children to follow.

4. Views. Each table has several view types. Public views are created by makers and shared with everyone who can read the table. System views have special jobs: Quick Find (which columns the search box searches and shows), Lookup (what users see when picking a row in a lookup), Associated (the list of related rows shown from the parent) and Advanced Find. Personal views belong to one user, who can share them. In a public view you set columns, column widths, filters and sort order, and you can set one public view as the default.

5. Main forms. A main form is built from tabs, sections and columns, plus a header and footer. Useful components include a subgrid (a list of related rows, such as comments), a quick view control (read-only details of a row selected in a lookup, using that table’s quick view form) and the timeline. Other form types are Quick Create (a short form that slides in for fast entry), Quick View and Card.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create the table chd_ticketcomment with a lookup chd_ticketid to Ticket. Set the behavior to Parental. Now deleting a ticket deletes its comments, and reassigning a ticket reassigns them.
  2. Open the Category-to-Ticket relationship (lookup chd_categoryid). Set it to Referential, Restrict Delete. A staff member who tries to delete the Wi-Fi category gets an error while tickets still use it.
  3. Add a self-referential lookup chd_parentticketid on Ticket for duplicate tickets, with Referential, Remove Link behavior.
  4. For followers, the team needs a date and a role per link, so create a custom intersect table chd_ticketfollower with lookups to Ticket and User.
  5. Create a public view High priority open tickets: filter Priority equals High and Status does not equal Closed, sort by Due date ascending.
  6. On the Ticket main form, add a Discussion tab with a Comments subgrid and a quick view control showing the Category’s owner team and description.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving every relationship on the default and discovering later that deleting a parent leaves orphaned rows or deletes too much.
  • Using a native N:N when the link needs its own data. A native intersect table cannot hold extra columns.
  • Thinking Parental only affects Delete. It cascades Assign, Share, Unshare, Reparent and Merge too.
  • Hiding a column on a form or view and calling it "secured". Forms and views are layout, not security.
  • Editing the Quick Find view columns and forgetting that its "find" columns control what search actually matches.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Must not be deleted if related records exist" points to Restrict Delete. "Children should be removed with the parent" points to Parental or Delete: Cascade All.
  • "Only move the active child records to the new owner" points to Custom with Assign: Cascade Active.
  • "Store extra information about the link" points to a manual many-to-many with a custom intersect table.
  • "Show details of the selected customer on this form without editing" points to a quick view control. "Show related rows on the form" points to a subgrid.

terms.definition: The rules that decide how actions on a parent row (delete, assign, share, unshare, reparent, merge) affect related child rows.
A one-to-many behavior where every action on the parent cascades to all related child rows.
A delete setting that blocks deleting a parent row while related child rows still exist.
The hidden or custom table that stores the pairs of rows in a many-to-many relationship.
A saved, shared view of a table with set columns, filters and sort order, available to every user with access to the table.
A read-only form of a related table shown inside another form through a lookup.

lessons.examTip: “Deleting the parent must also delete the children” means Parental (Delete: Cascade All). “Must not be deleted while children exist” means Restrict Delete.

quiz.question: Staff must never be able to delete a Category while any Ticket still uses it. Deleting a Ticket must not affect the Category. Which relationship behavior fits?
options: Many-to-many with a native intersect table
quiz.explanation: Restrict Delete blocks deleting the parent while child rows exist. Parental would delete tickets with the category; Remove Link would just clear the lookup.

quiz.question: When a Ticket is reassigned to another agent, all its Ticket Comments must be reassigned too. When a Ticket is deleted, its comments must be deleted. What is the simplest configuration?

Create a cloud flow for assign and a second flow for delete
Set the relationship to Referential, Remove Link
quiz.explanation: Parental cascades every action, including Assign and Delete, from the parent to all children with no extra logic.

quiz.question: Tickets and Staff members need a many-to-many link, and each link must store the date the staff member was added and their role on the ticket. What should you build?

A multi-select choice column on Ticket
quiz.explanation: A native N:N intersect table cannot hold extra columns. A custom intersect table (manual N:N) with two lookups can store the date and role.

quiz.question: Every agent should see a list of overdue open tickets from the Tickets page, without building it themselves. What should the maker create?
options: A personal view shared by each agent
A public view with filters on Due date and Status
quiz.explanation: Public views are shared, maker-defined views available to all users who can read the table. Personal views belong to one user.

lessons.title: Prompt columns and row summaries
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dataverse can now use generative AI directly on your data. A prompt column is a column with the data type Prompt. You write a natural-language prompt that references other columns in the row. When a row is created, or when a referenced column changes, the AI runs and stores the result in the column, so apps, flows and reports can use it.

  • Prompt columns consume credits each time the prompt executes; testing the prompt is free. Existing rows are not processed until one of their input columns changes.
  • A row summary is configured per table under Customizations. It shows an AI-generated summary of the record in a collapsible bar at the top of main forms and from an inline Summary action in views. It is generated when viewed, not stored in a column.
  • Row summaries need the AI insight cards environment setting; prompt columns need Copilot and AI prompts features turned on.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse now has two built-in ways to use generative AI on your rows without writing code or building a flow.

A prompt column is a column whose value is written by AI. You give it a prompt such as "Summarize this ticket in one sentence" and tell it which columns to read. When a row is created, or when one of those columns changes, the AI runs and the answer is saved in the column like any other data.

A row summary is a quick overview of the whole record that users see at the top of the form. The maker writes one prompt for the table. The summary is shown to the user in the app; it is not saved as a column.

Think of a hospital. The prompt column is the one-line diagnosis written into the patient’s file. The row summary is the nurse who reads the chart aloud when a doctor walks in.

Why it matters

Help desk tickets arrive with long, messy descriptions. Agents waste time reading. Managers want reports on themes, not raw text. Before these features, you needed a cloud flow that called an AI Builder prompt and wrote the result back. That meant more parts to build, secure and move between environments.

A prompt column puts that logic inside the table, so every app, flow, view and report sees the same stored result. A row summary helps people read records faster without adding any columns at all. AB-410 lists both under "Build data models", so expect design questions about which one fits.

How it works

Prompt columns

  • Create one: open a table, add a new column, choose the data type Prompt, clear Allow form fill assistance, then select Add new prompt. In the prompt editor, use +Add content to insert input columns. Test, save the prompt, then save the column.
  • Limit: up to five prompt columns per table.
  • When it runs: on row create, and on update of one or more input columns. If no input column changed, it does not run and no credits are used. It runs asynchronously, so the value can appear a moment after saving. There is no "run now" button.
  • Existing rows: not processed by default. Changing the prompt does not recalculate old values either; a row updates the next time one of its input columns changes.
  • Inputs: you can use several input columns. Formula, file, image and other prompt columns cannot be inputs; their values are ignored.
  • Filter conditions: you can apply a filter so the prompt runs only for rows that meet it, for example only High priority tickets. This saves credits.
  • Status tracking: the platform adds a status column and a details column. Status shows values such as not started, in progress, completed, skipped (filter not met or no input changed) and failed, with error details.
  • Prerequisites and cost: Copilot and AI prompts features must be on in the environment settings, and the Block unmanaged customizations setting must be off to create or edit them. Prompt columns use the same licensing model as AI Builder prompts; each execution consumes credits (AI Builder credits and Copilot Credits), and testing is free. Values are not audited.

Row summaries

  • Configure: open the table, and under Customizations select Row summary. Write a prompt, add columns with Add or by typing a slash, and describe the format you want, such as bullets with bold values.
  • Test: Test prompt uses the most recently edited row, so the table needs at least one row.
  • Apply: select Apply to main forms. The summary then shows on all main forms for that table.
  • User experience: a collapsible insights bar at the top of the main form (collapsed by default, with a one-line peek). Users can expand, Refresh, copy and give thumbs up or down. In views, an inline Summary action opens the summary in a popup. New rows show a summary only after they are saved.
  • Languages: include the LanguageCode input and tell the prompt to respond in that language.
  • Prerequisites: the AI insight cards environment setting must be on. Users of a Power Apps model-driven app need a Power Apps premium license.
  • Limits: not meant for calculations or date arithmetic; formula and calculated values, choice labels and related-row links may not be interpreted accurately. Not available on Case, Lead and Opportunity, which have their own Dynamics 365 summaries.
  • ALM: row summaries are solution-aware. You add them to a solution as an AI Skill Config component.
Prompt columnRow summaryAI Hub prompt in a flow
Result stored?Yes, in the rowNo, shown in the appOnly if the flow writes it
Runs whenRow created or input column changedUser opens or refreshesFlow trigger fires
Usable in reports and filtersYesNoIf written back
Best forEnriching data, such as a summary or a suggested categoryHelping users read a record fastMulti-step logic, other data sources, notifications
Remember: a prompt column is AI-generated, not deterministic. For exact rules, such as "Priority is High when Due date is today", use a formula column or business rule instead.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. In the Campus Help Desk solution, add a column chd_aisummary (AI summary) to Ticket with data type Prompt.
  2. Prompt: "Summarize the student’s problem in one sentence for a support agent. Then on a new line suggest one category from: Wi-Fi, Accounts, Printing, Classroom AV." Insert Title and Description with +Add content.
  3. Apply a filter so it runs only when Description has a value. Test with a sample, then save.
  4. Create a ticket: "Projector in room B12 shows no signal from HDMI." After a moment AI summary reads: "Classroom projector in B12 is not receiving an HDMI signal. Suggested category: Classroom AV."
  5. Add AI summary to the Active Tickets view so agents can scan tickets quickly. A cloud flow can also read it to alert the AV team.
  6. Configure a row summary on Ticket: bullets for Title, Priority, Status, Due date and Category, bold values, plus "You must respond in language LanguageCode". Apply to main forms.
  7. Add the AI Skill Config component to the solution so the row summary moves to test and production with the rest of the app.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting a new prompt column to fill in all existing rows. It only runs on create or when an input column changes.
  • Choosing a row summary when a report or flow needs the value. Row summaries are not stored data.
  • Referencing a formula column or another prompt column as input. Those inputs are ignored.
  • Forgetting the cost: every execution consumes credits. Use filter conditions and only the input columns you need.
  • Using AI for logic that must be exact and repeatable, such as SLA dates or totals.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Store", "use in a view, report or flow", "enrich data automatically when a row is created" point to a prompt column.
  • "Quick overview at the top of the form", "users refresh", "summary from the view" point to a row summary.
  • "Reduce AI credit consumption" or "only for some rows" point to filter conditions on the prompt column.
  • "Summary option is missing or not showing" often points to the AI insight cards setting or missing license; "cannot create a prompt column" can point to AI features being off or Block unmanaged customizations being on.

terms.definition: A Dataverse column of data type Prompt that runs a natural-language prompt on other columns in the row and stores the AI result.
A column referenced in the prompt; creating the row or changing one of these columns makes the prompt run again.
Optional conditions on a prompt column so the prompt runs only for rows that meet them, saving credits.
An AI-generated summary of a record, defined by a maker prompt on the table and shown on main forms and from views.
The environment feature setting that must be on for row summaries to appear.

lessons.examTip: “Store an AI result in the row for reports and flows” means prompt column. “Show users a quick overview of the record on the form” means row summary.

quiz.question: Managers want a short AI-generated summary of each ticket’s description stored in Dataverse so a Power BI report and a cloud flow can use it. What should you configure?
options: A row summary on the Ticket table
A prompt column on the Ticket table
A formula column using Power Fx

quiz.question: You add a prompt column to Ticket, which already has 5,000 rows. Next day, only new tickets and a few edited ones have a value. Why?
options: The prompt failed because of the 5,000-row limit

options: Row summary applied to main forms

lessons.title: Dataverse security in practice
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dataverse security is layered. Environment security groups decide who can enter the environment at all. Security roles decide what users can do with each table, and at what access level (User, Business Unit, Parent: Child Business Units, Organization). Business units group users and records so access can follow the organisation’s structure.

  • Teams can own records (owner teams), give ad-hoc access to single records (access teams), or mirror a Microsoft Entra ID group (group teams).
  • Sharing grants specific rights on one row to a user or team.
  • Column security protects sensitive columns through column security profiles, even when the user can read the row.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse security works like a campus building. The environment security group is the front gate: only people on the list get in. Security roles are the key cards: they say which rooms (tables) you can open and what you can do inside. Business units are the wings of the building: your card may open rooms only in your own wing. Teams are groups that share a card. Sharing is lending someone a key to one room. Column security is a locked drawer inside a room.

All layers apply together. A user needs to pass every one of them.

Why it matters

The Campus Help Desk now serves two campuses. Agents at North Campus should see North tickets, not City tickets. Managers should see both. Internal notes about staff conduct must be hidden from most agents. A contractor needs access to one ticket for a week. And only help desk staff should even be able to sign in to the production environment.

Getting this wrong has real cost: private data leaks, or agents who cannot do their work. AB-410 lists "configure security" under data models and asks you to apply it to realistic scenarios, not just define the words.

How it works

1. Environment security group. An admin can link a Microsoft Entra security group to a Dataverse environment in the Power Platform admin center. Only members of that group can be added as users. This decides who gets in; it does not decide what they can do. Without a security role, a user in the group still cannot work with data.

2. Business units. Every environment has a root business unit. You can create child units to form a hierarchy, such as Campus (root) with North Campus and City Campus below it. Every user and team belongs to one business unit. Every user- or team-owned row has an owner, and so belongs to a business unit.

3. Security roles. A role holds privileges per table and an access level for each privilege.

PrivilegeMeans
Create, Read, Write, DeleteBasic data actions on rows.
AppendAttach other rows to this row (for example set a lookup on this Ticket).
Append ToLet other rows be attached to this row (for example a Category that tickets point to).
AssignGive ownership of the row to someone else.
ShareGrant access to the row to another user or team.
Access levelRows covered
NoneNo rows.
UserRows the user owns, rows owned by their teams, and rows shared with them.
Business UnitAll rows in the user’s own business unit.
Parent: Child Business UnitsRows in the user’s unit and all units below it.
OrganizationAll rows in the environment.

Roles add up: if a user has two roles, they get the widest access from either one. Start from a copy of a standard role such as Basic User rather than building from nothing, because many system tables need at least read access for the app to work.

4. Teams.

Team typeOwns rows?Typical use
Owner teamYesA queue of work owned by a group, such as IT Support. Assign roles to the team; members get that access.
Access teamNoChanging groups per row. An access team template on a table lists the rights; members get them on that one row.
Microsoft Entra group teamOwner or access typeMembership follows an Entra security or Microsoft 365 group, so IT manages people in one place.

5. Sharing. A user with the Share privilege can share a single row with a user or team and choose rights such as Read, Write, Append, Assign, Share or Delete. Sharing is great for exceptions. It is poor as a main design, because many shares are hard to audit and can slow access checks.

6. Column security. Turn on column security for a column. Then create a column security profile that allows Read, Update and/or Create on that column, and add users or teams to it. Everyone else sees the column as empty or locked, in every app and API, even if they can read the row. System administrators always have access.

Watch out: hiding a column on a form, removing it from a view or making it read-only with a business rule is not security. Data can still be read through other views, exports or the API.

7. App access. For a model-driven app, the user also needs a security role that is assigned to the app. Canvas apps are shared with users or groups, but Dataverse roles still control the data behind them.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Gate: the admin links the Entra group HelpDesk-Staff to the production environment as its security group.
  2. Structure: business units Campus (root), North Campus and City Campus. Agents are placed in their campus unit; managers sit in the root unit.
  3. Help Desk Agent role: Ticket Create User, Read Business Unit, Write User, Append and Append To Business Unit; Category Read and Append To Organization. Agents see all tickets in their campus and edit their own.
  4. Help Desk Manager role: Ticket Read and Write Parent: Child Business Units, plus Assign. Managers in the root unit can see and reassign tickets in both campuses.
  5. Owner team IT Support in North Campus owns all network tickets. Members get the team’s role, so they can all work the queue.
  6. Access team template Ticket Collaborators on Ticket with Read and Write. For a complex outage, three agents are added to that ticket’s access team.
  7. Column security on chd_internalnotes, with a profile Help Desk Leads allowing Read and Update.
  8. Sharing: a contractor gets Read on one ticket, removed when the work is done.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the environment security group grants data access. It only controls who can be a user.
  • Confusing Append and Append To. To set a Category on a Ticket you need Append on Ticket and Append To on Category.
  • Giving Organization access "to make it work", which defeats business units.
  • Using sharing as the main security model instead of roles, business units and teams.
  • Believing a form change hides sensitive data. Only column security does.

How the exam asks about it

  • "See rows in their own department only" points to Business Unit access; "their department and all below it" points to Parent: Child Business Units.
  • "Group of people works a shared queue" points to an owner team; "different people per record" points to an access team; "membership managed in Entra ID" points to a group team.
  • "Specific field hidden from some users" points to column security.
  • "Restrict who can access the environment" points to an environment security group. "Can’t open the app" points to the app’s assigned security roles.

terms.definition: A security boundary that groups users, teams and records; units form a hierarchy under the root business unit.
How far a privilege reaches: None, User, Business Unit, Parent: Child Business Units or Organization.
A team that can own records and holds security roles, so its members share the team’s access.
A team created per record, often from an access team template, that grants the listed rights on that one record.
A set of Read, Update and Create permissions on secured columns, assigned to users or teams.
A Microsoft Entra security group linked to an environment so only its members can be added as users.

lessons.examTip: “Only people in this group should get into the environment” means an environment security group. “Hide one column from some users” means column security, not a view or form change.

options: Read Parent: Child Business Units, Write None
quiz.explanation: Business Unit read covers all rows owned in the user’s own unit. User write limits editing to rows the user or their teams own.

options: Remove the column from the main form

quiz.explanation: Column security protects the value everywhere, including APIs and exports. Hiding it on a form or view does not secure it.

quiz.question: Only members of the Entra group Help Desk Staff should be able to become users in the production environment. What should the admin configure?
quiz.explanation: Linking a Microsoft Entra security group to the environment restricts who can be added as a user. Roles then decide what those users can do.

options: A new business unit per ticket

quiz.explanation: Access teams give record-level rights to a changing group of users without creating owner teams or roles for each case.

domains.blurb: Model-driven apps, generative pages and dashboards, and professional canvas apps.

lessons.title: Compose model-driven apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
A model-driven app is composed, not drawn. In the modern app designer you add pages (Dataverse tables, dashboards, custom pages, web resources, URLs), arrange them in the navigation as groups and subareas, and pick which forms and views of each table the app includes.

  • Users need a security role that is assigned to the app, plus privileges on its tables, to open and use it.
  • Access to forms can be limited by security role; users without a matching role see the fallback form. Form order decides the default form.
  • Views available in the app come from the table’s public views that you include; users can still create personal views.
  • Save, publish, then share the app.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A model-driven app is built from parts that already exist in Dataverse: tables, forms, views, charts and dashboards. You do not place buttons pixel by pixel. You compose the app: you choose which parts to include, arrange them in a navigation menu and decide who can open it.

Think of a restaurant menu. The kitchen (Dataverse) already knows how to cook many dishes. The menu (the app) chooses which dishes to offer to which customers and in what order. Two menus can use the same kitchen: one for students, one for staff.

Why it matters

The Help Desk Staff app is used by agents and managers. Agents need a simple ticket screen and a short list of useful views. Managers need extra SLA fields and dashboards. Setup data such as Categories should be tucked away. A good composition makes the app fast to learn and hard to misuse.

Access matters too. The app should only open for staff, and the right form should appear for the right person without anyone choosing it. AB-410 covers this under "create model-driven apps", including access to forms, views and apps.

How it works

1. The app designer. Open the app from your solution in Power Apps. The modern app designer has a Pages pane, a Navigation pane, a preview canvas and a properties pane. You can also describe an app to Copilot to get a starting point, then refine it.

2. Page types.

Page typeWhat it showsHelp Desk use
Dataverse tableThe table’s views and formsTickets, Ticket Comments, Categories
DashboardSystem dashboards with charts and listsHelp desk overview for managers
Custom pageA canvas-style page built with Power FxA guided "triage" screen
Generative pageA page generated from a natural-language descriptionCovered in lesson A.9
Web resource / URLHTML or an external linkLink to the campus IT policy

3. Navigation (site map). Pages sit in groups as subareas. Larger apps can have several areas, which users switch between at the bottom of the left pane. You can rename groups, reorder subareas and hide pages from navigation.

4. Forms and views in the app. For each table page you choose which forms and views the app includes. You can include all of them, which also picks up new ones later, or select specific ones. Only public and system views can be included; users can still build personal views.

5. Access to forms. A table can have several main forms. You can assign security roles to a form, so only users with those roles can use it. The form order decides which allowed form opens first. A fallback form is shown to users who have no role matching any restricted form, so nobody is left without a form. Users with several allowed forms can switch using the form selector.

6. Access to the app. A model-driven app is shared through security roles. In the Share panel you assign one or more roles to the app and share it with users or teams. A user can run the app only if they have at least one role assigned to it. They also need privileges on the tables inside it, or they will see empty pages or errors.

QuestionWhere to control it
Can this user open the app?Security roles assigned to the app
Which form do they see?Form security roles, form order, fallback form
Which views appear in the selector?Views included in the app designer
Which rows and columns can they read or edit?Security roles, business units, column security

7. Save, publish, share. Saving keeps your changes as a draft. Publish makes them visible to users. Then share. Because the app is a solution component, it moves to test and production with its forms and views through your ALM process from lesson A.3.

Remember: app access and data access are separate. A role on the app lets the user in; roles on the tables decide what data they see.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Open Help Desk Staff in the app designer from the Campus Help Desk solution.
  2. Navigation: group Work with Tickets and Ticket Comments; group Insights with a Help Desk Overview dashboard; group Setup with Categories.
  3. For Tickets, include the main forms Ticket and Ticket - Manager, plus Quick Create Ticket. Include only the views Active Tickets, My Open Tickets and High priority open tickets.
  4. Restrict Ticket - Manager to the Help Desk Manager role. Put it first in the form order. Mark Ticket as the fallback form.
  5. Add a URL page that opens the campus IT policy.
  6. Save and Publish. Use Play to check that navigation, views and forms look right.
  7. Share: assign the Help Desk Agent and Help Desk Manager roles to the app, then share it with the HelpDesk-Staff team.
  8. Result: a manager opens a ticket and gets Ticket - Manager with SLA fields. An agent opens the same ticket and gets the simpler Ticket form.

Common mistakes

  • Sharing the app link without assigning a security role to the app. The user cannot open it.
  • Deleting unwanted views from the table instead of excluding them in the app, which breaks other apps.
  • Restricting every form by role and forgetting a fallback form, so some users see an unexpected form or none suited to them.
  • Forgetting to publish, then wondering why users do not see the new navigation.
  • Treating form restriction as data security. A user who cannot see a form can still read the row in other ways.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Different users should see different forms" points to form security roles plus form order and a fallback form.
  • "Only show certain views in this app" points to including specific views in the app designer.
  • "User received the link but cannot open the app" points to security roles assigned to the app.
  • "Add a page with custom layout built in Power Fx" points to a custom page; "organise the left menu" points to navigation groups and subareas.

terms.definition: The Power Apps tool where you compose a model-driven app from pages, navigation, forms and views.
The app’s navigation structure of areas, groups and subareas that users see in the left pane.
The order of main forms for a table; users get the first form their security roles allow.
The form shown to users whose security roles do not match any role-restricted form.
The security roles assigned to a model-driven app; only users with one of them can run it.

lessons.examTip: “User can’t open the app although the link was shared” usually means their security role is not assigned to the app.

options: Two apps with the same name

quiz.explanation: Main forms can be restricted by security role. Users without a matching role get the fallback form.
