options: The app navigation (site map) groups and subareas
quiz.explanation: Navigation groups and subareas in the app designer define the site map that users see in the left pane.

lessons.title: Generative pages, charts and dashboards
lessons.summaryHtml:
Model-driven apps are built mostly from forms and views, but three more page types add power. A generative page is a custom page that an AI agent writes for you as React code from a plain-English description, optional images and up to six Dataverse tables. Charts turn the rows of a view into a visual summary, and dashboards put several charts, lists and Power BI content on one page.

  • Add a generative page in the app designer with Add page then Generative page, then iterate by chatting or by editing the code.
  • System charts and dashboards are part of the solution and shared by everyone. Personal ones belong to one user until shared.
  • Charts always work on top of a view, so the view decides which rows are counted.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A model-driven app is built from pages. Most pages are forms (one record) and views (lists of records). Three more page types help staff see the big picture and work faster.

A generative page is a custom page that AI writes for you. You describe what you want in plain English, pick the Dataverse tables it should use and, if you like, attach a sketch. An app agent then writes the page as React code. React is a popular JavaScript library for building web user interfaces.

A chart is a picture of the rows in a view, such as a bar for each category. A dashboard is a page that places several charts, lists and reports side by side.

Think of a hospital ward. Forms are individual patient files. Views are the patient list. Charts are the bed-occupancy graph on the wall. The dashboard is the whole wall board the nurse checks at the start of a shift. A generative page is a special tool the ward manager asked a carpenter to build, just by describing it.

Why it matters

Staff at the Campus Help Desk open the app every morning. They need to know at a glance how many tickets are open, which categories are busy and which tickets are urgent. Clicking through lists takes too long. A dashboard answers these questions in seconds.

Sometimes the standard pages are not enough. A manager may want a triage board with cards grouped by priority. In the past this needed a developer to write a custom page or a PCF control. With generative pages a maker can describe it and get working code, then refine it by chatting. On AB-410 you must know when a generative page is the right choice and how to build and publish one.

How it works

1. Generative pages. In the app designer you select Add page, then Generative page, then Describe a page. You provide:

  • A description of the page: what it should show and do, plus any layout wishes.
  • Data: up to six Dataverse tables that the page can read and write.
  • Optional images, from a rough napkin sketch to a finished mock-up, to guide the look.

The app agent generates React code for both the user interface and the business logic. You preview it, then keep chatting to fix errors, change the layout or add features. The Code tab shows the generated code, and you can edit it by hand. When you are happy, Save and Publish publishes the app including the page. Generative pages became generally available in late 2025. Prompts must be in English, and the environment must be in one of the supported regions, so check the current list on Microsoft Learn. Only one maker should edit a generative page at a time.

Remember: a generative page is still part of the model-driven app and the solution. It uses Dataverse security, so users only see rows their security role allows.

2. Charts. A chart is defined on a table and always displays the rows of a view. The user opens a view, selects Show chart and picks a chart. If the view shows only active tickets, the chart counts only active tickets.

Chart typeGood forHelp Desk example
Column or barComparing counts across categoriesTickets per category
Stacked columnA second breakdown inside each barTickets per category, split by priority
Line or areaTrends over timeNew tickets per week
Pie or doughnutShare of a whole with few slicesTickets by status
FunnelStages of a processTickets at each stage of a process flow

In the chart designer you choose the legend (series) column and the axis (category) column, and an aggregation such as count, sum or average.

3. System and personal.

System chart or dashboardPersonal chart or dashboard
Created byA maker, in the solutionAny user, inside the running app
Who sees itEveryone who can use the table or appThe owner, plus people it is shared with
ALMMoves with the solution to test and productionStored as user data, not in the solution
Typical useStandard reporting for a teamA user’s own analysis

4. Dashboards. A classic dashboard is a grid of components: charts, lists (views), web resources and, where the environment allows it, Power BI content. Users can also embed Power BI tiles in personal dashboards. Interactive dashboards are designed for people who work queues all day. They show streams of records and tiles that filter the page when clicked. You add a dashboard to an app in the app designer as a Dashboard page.

Watch out: adding a table to the app does not automatically show every chart and dashboard to users. Check which components are included in the app and publish after changes.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The staff lead asks for a triage board. In Help Desk Staff, select Add page, Generative page, Describe a page. The description is: “Show open tickets as cards in three columns by Priority (High, Medium, Low). Each card shows Title, Category and Due date. A button sets Status to In progress.”
  2. Add the Ticket and Category tables. Attach a photo of a whiteboard sketch of the three columns.
  3. The agent generates the page. In preview, the cards appear. The lead asks: “Highlight cards whose Due date is before today in red.” The agent updates the code.
  4. In the solution, open the Ticket table, then Charts. Create a stacked column chart: axis Category, legend Priority, aggregation count of Title. Name it “Tickets by category and priority”.
  5. Create a view “Open tickets” with the filter Status equals Open. Staff open this view and show the chart, so it counts only open tickets.
  6. Create a system dashboard “Help Desk Overview” with the chart, a pie chart of tickets by status and a list of the Open tickets view.
  7. Add the dashboard and the generative page to the app navigation. Save and Publish, then export the solution so both move to test.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a chart has its own filter. The view decides which rows the chart counts.
  • Building a team dashboard as a personal dashboard. Personal items do not travel in the solution, so they never reach production.
  • Assuming a generative page is a canvas app. It is React code inside the model-driven app.
  • Choosing a generative page for a simple list. A view or a form is simpler, faster and easier to maintain.
  • Forgetting to publish. New charts and pages are not visible to users until the app and customisations are published.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Describe the page in natural language”, “attach a sketch” or “no developer available for a custom UI” point to a generative page.
  • “Only the user who created it” or “share with a colleague” point to personal charts or dashboards. “Must move with the solution” points to system ones.
  • “Chart shows the wrong rows” points to the view the chart is shown with.
  • “Agents work a queue and filter by clicking tiles” points to an interactive dashboard.

terms.definition: A model-driven app page that an app agent generates as React code from a natural-language description, data and optional images.
A chart defined by a maker on a table, stored in the solution and available to all users of that table.
A chart a user creates for themselves; it can be shared with other users or teams.
A page that combines charts, lists (views), web resources or Power BI content in a grid layout.
A dashboard type with filterable streams and tiles, designed for users who work queues all day.

lessons.examTip: “Describe the page in words and let AI build it” means a generative page. “Visual summary of the rows in a view” means a chart. “Several visuals on one landing page” means a dashboard.

quiz.question: A manager wants a custom triage page in Help Desk Staff with drag-and-drop cards. Nobody on the team writes code. Which option fits best?
options: A main form with extra tabs

quiz.explanation: A generative page is created by describing it in plain English; the app agent writes the React code and you iterate by chatting.

options: Share the personal chart with the colleagues

quiz.question: A chart “Tickets by category” shows closed tickets too, but staff only want open tickets. What controls which rows the chart counts?
options: The view the chart is displayed with
quiz.explanation: A chart summarises the rows returned by the current view. Choose or create a view that filters to open tickets.

quiz.question: You add a generative page to the app. Which statement is correct?
options: It can only use SharePoint data
It is a canvas app embedded with an iframe

quiz.explanation: Generative pages accept a description, up to six Dataverse tables and optional images. The result is React code that you can view, edit or refine by chat.

lessons.title: Canvas apps: data, variables and collections
lessons.summaryHtml:
Canvas apps hold state in variables and collections. Set creates a global variable, UpdateContext creates a context variable for one screen, and Navigate can pass context variables to the next screen. Collections are in-memory tables you fill with ClearCollect and Collect and trim with Remove.

  • Patch creates or updates a record in a data source such as the Dataverse Ticket table.
  • Delegation means the data source runs the query. If a function cannot be delegated, the app only looks at the first 500 rows by default (up to 2,000 if you change the setting) and shows a delegation warning.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A canvas app needs to remember things while it runs: who the user is, which ticket they picked, what they have put in a basket. It remembers them in variables and collections.

A variable holds one value, such as a number, a text or a whole record. A collection holds a table of rows, like a small spreadsheet that lives only in the app’s memory.

Think of a student’s desk. A sticky note on the wall that you can see from anywhere in the room is a global variable. A note inside one notebook is a context variable: it only matters on that page. A tray of papers is a collection. The college filing cabinet is the real data source, such as the Dataverse Ticket table.

Delegation is about who does the searching. If the filing cabinet has a clerk who searches for you, you get correct answers from every drawer. If not, you carry the first few hundred files to your desk and search there, and you miss the rest.

Why it matters

Most canvas app bugs come from state and data. A value set on one screen is missing on another. A gallery shows 500 tickets when there are 12,000. A Save button creates a duplicate instead of updating a record. The AB-410 outline lists “variables and collections” and delegation is tested often, because a wrong choice gives wrong results without an obvious error.

How it works

1. Three kinds of variables.

KindCreated byScopeExample
Global variableSetEvery screenSet(varCampus, "North")
Context variableUpdateContext, or Navigate with a recordOne screenUpdateContext({locEdit: true})
CollectionCollect, ClearCollectEvery screenClearCollect(colSaved, ...)

Variables are created the first time a formula sets them, and their type comes from the first value. A common naming habit is var for global, loc for context and col for collections.

// Global: whole app
Set(varMe, User());
// Context: this screen only
UpdateContext({locEdit: true, locCount: 0});
// Pass context to the next screen
Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover, {locTicket: ThisItem})

The third argument of Navigate creates or updates context variables on the target screen. On scrDetail you can then use locTicket.Title.

2. Collections. Collect adds rows. ClearCollect removes all rows and then adds new ones. Clear empties a collection. Remove deletes specific rows, and RemoveIf deletes rows that match a condition. Collections are useful for offline drafts, baskets and caching small lookup tables such as Categories.

ClearCollect(colCategories, Categories);
Collect(colSaved, galTickets.Selected);
Remove(colSaved, ThisItem);
RemoveIf(colSaved, Priority = 'Priority (Tickets)'.Low)

3. Patch. Patch writes to a data source. The second argument decides whether it creates or updates.

// Create a new ticket
Patch(Tickets, Defaults(Tickets),
  {Title: txtTitle.Text, Description: txtDesc.Text,
   Priority: 'Priority (Tickets)'.Medium,
   Category: drpCategory.Selected});
// Update the selected ticket
Patch(Tickets, galTickets.Selected,
  {Priority: 'Priority (Tickets)'.High})

Choice columns take an option from the choice, such as the High option. Lookup columns take a record from the related table. Patch returns the saved record, so you can store it: Set(varNew, Patch(...)). Forms with SubmitForm are simpler for standard edit screens; Patch is best when you need custom layouts or to save several things at once.

4. Delegation. When a formula such as Filter, Sort or Search can be translated into a query the data source understands, the data source does the work on all rows. That is delegation. When it cannot, Power Apps downloads only the first rows up to the data row limit, 500 by default and at most 2,000, then processes them locally. The designer shows a delegation warning: a yellow triangle and a blue underline on the formula.

Formula on DataverseDelegable?
Filter(Tickets, Priority = 'Priority (Tickets)'.High)Yes, a simple comparison
Filter(Tickets, StartsWith(Title, txtSearch.Text))Yes
SortByColumns(Tickets, "createdon", SortOrder.Descending)Yes
Filter(Tickets, Len(Title) > 20)No, Len is processed locally

Which functions delegate depends on the data source. Dataverse and SQL Server support many, while Excel files do not delegate at all. Always read the warning and check the delegation list for your connector.

Watch out: raising the data row limit to 2,000 hides the problem in testing but does not fix it. With more rows the results are still incomplete. Rewrite the formula so it delegates.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. App.OnStart has Set(varMe, User()). The home screen label shows "Hello " & varMe.FullName.
  2. The My tickets gallery shows the student’s own tickets, newest first: 
    SortByColumns(
  Filter(Tickets, 'Created By'.'Primary Email' = varMe.Email),
  "createdon", SortOrder.Descending)
  3. OnSelect of the gallery: Navigate(scrDetail, ScreenTransition.Cover, {locTicket: ThisItem}). The detail screen shows locTicket.Title and locTicket.Description.
  4. A toggle on scrDetail runs UpdateContext({locEdit: Self.Value}). Text inputs use If(locEdit, DisplayMode.Edit, DisplayMode.View).
  5. The Save button runs Patch(Tickets, locTicket, {Description: txtDesc.Text}) and then UpdateContext({locEdit: false}).
  6. Students can bookmark tickets with Collect(colSaved, ThisItem). The Saved screen lists colSaved with a Remove icon.
  7. A tester adds Filter(Tickets, Len(Title) > 20) to find long titles, sees the delegation warning and replaces it with a view-based or server-side approach instead.

Common mistakes

  • Using UpdateContext and expecting the value on another screen. Use Set, or pass it with Navigate.
  • Using Collect in OnVisible, so rows pile up every visit. Use ClearCollect.
  • Patching with Defaults when you meant to update, which creates duplicates.
  • Ignoring delegation warnings because test data has only 50 rows.
  • Copying a whole large table into a collection “for speed”. Collections are not delegable and are limited by the data row limit.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Available on all screens” points to Set. “Only on this screen” points to UpdateContext. “Pass the selected item to the next screen” points to Navigate with a context record.
  • “Replace” or “refresh the list” points to ClearCollect; “add to the list” points to Collect.
  • “Create or update a record without a form” points to Patch; Defaults means create.
  • “Only 500 rows”, “missing records” or “yellow triangle” point to delegation.

terms.definition: A variable created with Set that every screen of the app can read.
A variable created with UpdateContext or passed by Navigate that exists only on one screen.
An in-memory table in the app, created with Collect or ClearCollect.
A function that creates or modifies records in a data source or collection.
Sending the filter, sort or search to the data source so it processes all rows, not just the first few hundred.
The number of rows a non-delegable query brings back, 500 by default and at most 2,000.

lessons.examTip: “Available on every screen” means Set. “Only this screen” means UpdateContext. “Replace the contents” means ClearCollect. A yellow triangle on Filter means a delegation problem.

steps: Download the exercise files. Open the student canvas app and check that Tickets and Categories are added as data sources.

Create four screens: scrHome, scrNew, scrDetail and scrSaved. Add the controls named in state-and-data.txt from the start folder (galTickets, lblHello, lblCount, icoSave, drpCategory, btnSubmit, lblTitle, tglEdit, txtDetailDesc, btnSave, galSaved, icoRemove).
Work through state-and-data.txt from the start folder top to bottom and replace each TODO with your own formula.
Run App.OnStart (right-click App > Run OnStart), then play scrHome and check the gallery and count against the check list below.
Paste the delegation experiment formula into galTickets.Items, read the warning, then undo it.
Submit a new ticket, open a ticket on scrDetail, edit its description with the toggle, and save two tickets for later then remove one.
Compare your formulas with state-and-data.txt in the solution folder and fix any differences that change behaviour.
check: galTickets shows 4 tickets in this order: CHD-1017, CHD-1014, CHD-1009, CHD-1002, and lblCount reads “4 tickets”.
The formula Filter(Tickets, Len(Title) > 20) shows a delegation warning and 26 rows; only CHD-1011 and CHD-1023 have titles of 20 characters or fewer.
A ticket submitted from scrNew appears in the Ticket table with Priority Medium and Status Open, and the table has one more row than before (29 if you started with the 28 rows of tickets.csv).
Saving the same ticket twice leaves one row in colSaved (check it under Variables > Collections).
After Save on scrDetail the ticket description is updated in place, and the Ticket table still has the same number of rows.

quiz.question: The student app must remember the selected campus on every screen after the user picks it on the home screen. Which function should you use?
quiz.explanation: Set creates a global variable that every screen can read. UpdateContext only works on the current screen.

quiz.question: A gallery shows tickets with Filter(Tickets, Len(Title) > 20). There are 12,000 tickets and the gallery shows fewer than expected, with a warning icon. What is the cause?
options: The Ticket table needs a relationship
The gallery needs a flexible height
Len cannot be delegated, so only the first rows up to the data row limit are checked
quiz.explanation: Len is not delegable to Dataverse. The app downloads only up to the data row limit and filters those rows locally, so results are incomplete.

quiz.question: A button must update the Priority of the ticket selected in galTickets to High. Which formula is correct?
quiz.explanation: Patch with an existing record as the second argument updates that record in the data source. In a real app the value is the choice option, for example the High option of the Priority choice.

quiz.question: Every time a user opens the Saved screen, the list must be reloaded fresh from the data source, with no old rows left behind. What should OnVisible use?
quiz.explanation: ClearCollect empties the collection and then fills it again. Collect only adds rows, so old rows would stay.

lessons.title: Canvas apps: reusable components and design quality
lessons.summaryHtml:
Associate makers build canvas apps that are easy to reuse, work on any screen size, and are fast and accessible. Components package controls and logic with custom properties. Component libraries share components across apps. Named formulas in App.Formulas and user-defined functions share logic inside one app.

  • Responsive apps turn off Scale to fit and use horizontal and vertical containers with formulas based on Parent.Width.
  • Accessible apps set AccessibleLabel, a sensible tab order and good contrast, and pass the accessibility checker.
  • Fast apps move work out of App.OnStart into named formulas, run independent loads with Concurrent, and use delegable queries.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A beginner builds each screen by hand and copies formulas around. An associate maker builds once and reuses. They also make sure the app works on any screen, for every user, and opens quickly.

Think of building houses. Components are prefabricated windows: designed once, fitted in many rooms. A component library is the factory catalogue that many building sites order from. Named formulas are facts written on the site noticeboard that everyone reads. User-defined functions are standard instructions, like “how to fit a door”, that take inputs and give a result. Containers are flexible walls that stretch to fit the plot.

Why it matters

The Campus Help Desk now has a student app, a staff tool and a feedback app. All three need the same header and colour rules. Without reuse, a logo change means editing three apps by hand. Students use phones, tablets and laptops, and some use screen readers. The college also has a rule that apps must open in a few seconds. AB-410 tests reusable components, named formulas, user-defined functions and design for accessibility, performance and responsiveness.

How it works

1. Components. A component is a group of controls with custom properties:

  • Input properties receive values from the app, such as a Title text.
  • Output properties expose values to the app, such as IsMenuOpen.
  • Behavior properties are events the app can handle, such as OnBack, like OnSelect on a button.

By default a component cannot see the app’s data sources or variables. It should get what it needs through input properties. This keeps it reusable. A component setting can give it access to app scope when needed.

2. Component libraries. A component library is a special app that only holds components. You publish it, then import components into apps. When the library changes and is published again, apps that use it are notified and the maker can accept the update. Libraries can be included in solutions.

3. Named formulas. In the app’s Formulas property you write name = formula; pairs. They are calculated when first needed and always stay up to date, so there is no timing problem.

ThemeBlue = ColorValue("#1F4E9A");
MeUser = LookUp(Users, 'Primary Email' = User().Email);
OpenCount = CountRows(Filter(Tickets, 'Created By'.User = MeUser.User))

4. User-defined functions. Also in App.Formulas, a user-defined function has typed parameters and a return type. A function with side effects, such as Set or Patch, uses Void and curly braces. You can define your own types with Type.

DueLabel(d: Date): Text =
  If(d < Today(), "Overdue", "Due " & Text(d, "dd mmm"));

MarkInProgress(t: Text): Void = {
  Patch(Tickets, LookUp(Tickets, Title = t),
    {Status: 'Status (Tickets)'.'In progress'})
};
NeedBest tool
Same UI and behaviour on many screens of one appComponent
Same UI across several apps, updated centrallyComponent in a component library
A value used in many formulasNamed formula
Reusable logic with inputs and a resultUser-defined function
A value that the user changes while the app runsVariable (Set)

5. Responsive design. Turn off Scale to fit in the display settings so the app uses the real screen size. Then use horizontal and vertical containers, which arrange children in a row or column and can wrap or stretch. Size controls with formulas such as Parent.Width, and use App.ActiveScreen.Size or App.Width to switch layout at breakpoints. A gallery can use flexible height for rows of different sizes.

6. Accessibility. Set AccessibleLabel on icons, images and inputs so screen readers can describe them. Keep a logical tab order, use strong colour contrast, never rely on colour alone (add text such as “High”), and make touch targets large enough. Run the App checker, which lists accessibility issues along with formula and performance hints.

7. Performance.

  • Avoid heavy App.OnStart logic. Microsoft recommends named formulas where possible, because they calculate on demand and do not block the first screen.
  • Use Concurrent to run independent loads at the same time.
  • Use delegable queries and load only the columns and rows you need.
  • Keep the number of controls per screen reasonable and cache small lookup tables.
  • Use App.StartScreen to choose the first screen instead of Navigate in OnStart.
Concurrent(
  ClearCollect(colCategories, Categories),
  Set(varSettings, LookUp(Settings, Name = "Default"))
)
Remember: variables set in OnStart are not available in App.StartScreen, but named formulas are.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create the component library “Campus UI” in the solution. Build cmpHeader with input Title, output IsMenuOpen and behavior OnBack. Set the header fill to an input property Colour so each app can pass its theme.
  2. Publish the library and import cmpHeader into the student app and the feedback app. On each screen, set Title and OnBack: Back().
  3. In App.Formulas of the student app, add ThemeBlue, MeUser and DueLabel from above. Replace every copy of the colour code with ThemeBlue.
  4. Turn off Scale to fit. The home screen becomes a vertical container with the header, a horizontal container for filter buttons and a gallery with flexible height.
  5. Set AccessibleLabel on the “escalate” icon to "Escalate this ticket". Show priority as text and colour, not colour alone.
  6. Move category and settings loading out of OnStart into named formulas, and wrap the remaining loads in Concurrent. Compare load time before and after with Monitor.

Common mistakes

  • Letting a component read app variables directly, which breaks reuse. Pass data through input properties.
  • Using Set in OnStart for a value that never changes. A named formula is simpler and faster.
  • Expecting a named formula to change like a variable. It is a definition; it recalculates only when its inputs change.
  • Building responsive layouts with fixed X and Y values while Scale to fit is still on.
  • Adding a Tooltip and thinking it replaces AccessibleLabel.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Several apps” and “update in one place” point to a component library.
  • “Reusable calculation with parameters” points to a user-defined function; “constant or derived value used everywhere” points to a named formula.
  • “App is slow to open” points to moving OnStart logic to named formulas and using Concurrent.
  • “Screen reader” points to AccessibleLabel; “phones and tablets” points to containers with Scale to fit off.

terms.definition: A reusable group of controls with its own input, output and behavior properties.
A special app that stores components so many apps can import them and receive updates.
A formula defined once in App.Formulas, calculated when needed and always up to date.
A function you write in App.Formulas with typed parameters and a return type.
A control that lays out its child controls horizontally or vertically so they adapt to screen size.
A function that runs several formulas at the same time to shorten loading.

lessons.examTip: “Share the same header across many apps” means a component library. “Reusable calculation inside one app” means a named formula or a user-defined function. “Slow start” means move logic out of OnStart.

Every row in galTickets shows “Overdue”, because every Due Date in tickets.csv is on or before 3 Sep 2026.
lblOpen shows 6 open tickets, plus any tickets with Status Open you created in A.10.
If you imported tickets.csv yourself, MyOpenTickets returns 12 rows (6 Open and 6 In progress), plus the tickets you submitted in A.10.
The App checker lists 0 accessibility issues, and on scrHome the header’s back icon is hidden.

quiz.question: Three different canvas apps need the same header with the campus logo. When the logo changes, all apps should get the update. What should you build?
options: A named formula in each app
A component in a component library
quiz.explanation: Component libraries store components centrally. Apps that import them are notified of updates and can accept them.

quiz.question: App.OnStart loads categories, the current user and settings one after another, and the app is slow to open. What does Microsoft recommend first?
options: Move the logic into named formulas in App.Formulas where possible
Increase the data row limit to 2,000
Put the same logic in every screen OnVisible
quiz.explanation: Microsoft guidance says OnStart can slow loading; named formulas are calculated only when needed and are always up to date. Concurrent can help for work that must stay in OnStart.

quiz.question: A screen-reader user cannot tell what the “escalate” icon does. Which property should you set?
quiz.explanation: Screen readers read AccessibleLabel. Every icon and image that has a meaning needs one.

quiz.question: The app looks fine on a laptop but controls overflow on a phone. The app has Scale to fit turned on. What should you do?
options: Turn off Scale to fit and use containers with formulas based on Parent.Width
Add a second copy of every screen
Set every control X and Y to 0
Use a gallery on every screen
quiz.explanation: Responsive design starts with turning off Scale to fit, then using horizontal and vertical containers and relative sizes so the layout adapts.

lessons.title: Canvas apps: errors, testing, flows and agents
lessons.summaryHtml:
A production canvas app handles errors, is tested, and hands heavy work to flows and agents. IfError catches an error in a formula and runs a fallback. Notify shows a banner message. App.OnError is one central place to log or report errors. Errors() returns the errors from the last change to a data source.

  • Monitor records every event, formula and network call while you use the app, which helps with slow screens and delegation.
  • Test Studio records and runs automated test cases inside Power Apps. The older Power Apps Test Engine was deprecated in April 2026; Microsoft now points to Playwright samples.
  • Canvas apps call cloud flows with the Power Apps (V2) trigger and .Run(), and makers can generate a Copilot Studio agent from a canvas app with agent builder (preview).
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A demo app works when everything goes right. A production app also behaves well when things go wrong, is tested before each release, and hands long jobs to other tools.

Think of a bus service. Error handling is the driver’s plan for a flat tyre. Notify is the announcement to passengers. App.OnError is the depot’s incident log. Monitor is the vehicle tracker that shows every stop and delay. Test Studio is the test drive before a new route opens. A cloud flow is a courier the driver calls for a heavy parcel, and a Copilot Studio agent is a help point that answers passengers’ questions.

Why it matters

If a ticket save fails at the Campus Help Desk, the student sees a red banner with a technical message and may think the ticket was sent. Staff never learn about the failure. When the gallery gets slow, nobody knows why. When a new version ships, a broken Submit button is found by users, not testers. The AB-410 outline asks you to implement error handling, test apps with tools including Monitor, automate business processes from canvas apps and create a Copilot Studio agent from a canvas app.

How it works

1. IfError and Notify. IfError runs a formula. If it returns an error, IfError runs the replacement formula instead. Inside the replacement, FirstError describes the first error and AllErrors lists all of them. An optional last argument runs when there was no error. Notify shows a banner with a type from NotificationType (Success, Information, Warning, Error) and an optional timeout in milliseconds.

IfError(
  Patch(Tickets, Defaults(Tickets),
    {Title: txtTitle.Text, Description: txtDesc.Text}),
  Notify("Ticket not saved: " & FirstError.Message,
    NotificationType.Error),
  Notify("Ticket submitted", NotificationType.Success, 3000);
  Navigate(scrHome)
)

2. Errors() for data sources. After Patch or SubmitForm fails, Errors(Tickets) returns a table of problems, each with a Column, Message and Error kind. You can show these messages next to fields or check that the table is empty. An Error function lets you raise your own error, for example when validation fails.

3. App.OnError. This property runs whenever an error is not handled by IfError or similar. Use it to log the error, for example with Trace or by writing to a log table. Microsoft notes that OnError controls how errors are reported; it cannot replace a value in a calculation the way IfError can. If you want the default banner as well, re-raise the error with Error(FirstError).

Trace("Error in " & FirstError.Source & ": " & FirstError.Message,
  TraceSeverity.Error);
Error(FirstError)
ToolScopeUse it to
IfErrorOne formulaCatch and replace an error, show a message
Errors(source)One data sourceRead why the last save failed
App.OnErrorWhole appLog or report every unhandled error
NotifyUser interfaceTell the user what happened

4. Monitor. Monitor records a live log of the app while you use it: events, formula evaluations, network calls to connectors and Dataverse, their durations and any errors. You open it from Advanced tools in Power Apps Studio or for a published app, and you can invite a colleague to join a session to see what happens in their app. Trace calls also appear here. Use it to find slow calls, repeated requests and delegation issues.

5. Testing. Test Studio is built into Power Apps. You group test cases into test suites. A test case is a series of steps written in Power Fx, such as Select(btnSubmit) and SetProperty(txtTitle.Text, "Wi-Fi down"), plus Assert statements that must be true. You can record steps by using the app, play tests back in the browser and run them in a deployment pipeline. Some controls, such as components and PCF code components, are not supported.

The Power Apps Test Engine was an open-source tool that ran Power Fx test plans outside the studio. Microsoft deprecated it in April 2026 and now recommends the Power Platform Playwright samples for automated browser testing. Know the name, but expect Test Studio and Monitor to be the main answers for canvas apps.

6. Calling cloud flows. Heavy or background work, such as emailing a team, calling an external system or updating many rows, belongs in a cloud flow. The flow uses the Power Apps (V2) trigger with typed inputs. To send data back, it ends with Respond to a Power App or flow. In the studio, add the flow from the Power Automate pane, then call it with .Run().

Set(varEsc, EscalateTicket.Run(Text(galTickets.Selected.Ticket)));
Notify(varEsc.message, NotificationType.Information)

The flow runs as the user who pressed the button, using that user’s connections unless the flow is set up otherwise. Put both the app and the flow in the same solution.

7. Agents and canvas apps. Agent builder (preview) can create a Copilot Studio agent starting from an existing canvas app. It reads the app’s metadata and your goal, drafts step-by-step instructions, and extracts knowledge, triggers and actions from the app. You then edit, test and publish the agent in Copilot Studio. The feature is still rolling out, so it may not be in every region. For embedding chat inside an app, note that from February 2026 the older Copilot control can no longer be added to new canvas apps; Microsoft points makers to Microsoft 365 Copilot in Power Apps, which can be customised with agents.

Watch out: preview features change quickly. Describe them at the level of “generate an agent from the app, then refine it in Copilot Studio” rather than memorising exact buttons.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The Submit button wraps Patch in IfError, shows a success banner and navigates home, or shows FirstError.Message as an error banner.
  2. App.OnError writes the error message, screen and user email to a chd_applog table with Patch, then re-raises it so the user still sees a banner.
  3. Staff report a slow gallery. The maker opens Monitor, repeats the steps and sees the same Dataverse request sent three times from different OnVisible formulas. They move it to a named formula.
  4. In Test Studio the maker creates a suite “Submit ticket” with a case that sets the title and description, selects Submit, then runs Assert(IsEmpty(Errors(Tickets)), "Save succeeded").
  5. A flow EscalateTicket uses the Power Apps (V2) trigger with input TicketId, updates Priority to High, posts to the staff Teams channel and responds with message "Escalated". The app calls EscalateTicket.Run(...).
  6. The maker tries agent builder on the student app. The draft agent suggests actions to create and look up tickets. They compare it with Help Desk Assistant and copy the useful actions.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting App.OnError to replace a failed value. Only IfError replaces results; OnError reports.
  • Checking Errors() on the wrong data source, or before the save has run.
  • Using an automated or scheduled trigger for a flow that the app must start. Canvas apps need the Power Apps (V2) trigger.
  • Forgetting the Respond to a Power App or flow action, so .Run() returns nothing useful.
  • Treating Test Engine as the current recommended tool. It is deprecated; Test Studio and Playwright are the paths today.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Friendly message” or “continue if the save fails” points to IfError with Notify.
  • “Log all errors centrally” points to App.OnError; “which column failed validation” points to Errors().
  • “Slow”, “network calls” or “troubleshoot a user’s session live” point to Monitor. “Automated regression tests” and “Assert” point to Test Studio.
  • “Return a value to the app” points to Power Apps (V2) plus Respond to a Power App or flow. “Build an agent from an existing app” points to agent builder and Copilot Studio.

terms.definition: Runs a formula and, if it returns an error, runs a replacement formula instead.
Shows a banner message to the user with a type such as Success, Warning or Error.
An app property that runs whenever an unhandled error happens, for logging or custom reporting.
Returns a table of errors for a data source after Patch or SubmitForm failed.
A tool that shows a live log of app events, formulas and data calls for troubleshooting.
The built-in tool for recording, writing and running automated tests for canvas apps.

quiz.question: When a ticket fails to save, users should see a clear message instead of the default red banner, and the rest of the formula should not run. What should you use?
options: IfError around the Patch with Notify in the fallback
quiz.explanation: IfError catches the error from Patch and lets you run Notify with a friendly message as the replacement result.

quiz.question: The team wants every unhandled error in the app written to a log table, without editing each button. Where should the logic go?

quiz.question: The ticket gallery takes several seconds to load and you suspect a slow data call. Which tool shows each network request and its duration?

lessons.title: Cloud flows: triggers, connectors and actions
lessons.summaryHtml:
A cloud flow is a trigger followed by actions. At associate level you must pick the right trigger for a requirement, choose connectors with licensing and governance in mind, and configure actions so they do exactly the work needed and no more.

  • Automated triggers react to events (a Dataverse row changes, an email arrives). Instant triggers start on request (a button, a canvas app). Scheduled triggers run on a Recurrence.
  • The Dataverse trigger When a row is added, modified or deleted lets you set change type, table, scope, Select columns and Filter rows so the flow only runs when it should.
  • Trigger conditions in the trigger settings add a final expression check before a run starts.
  • Connectors are standard, premium or custom. Dataverse is premium. Data policies group connectors so business data cannot leak to the wrong services.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A cloud flow is a small robot with a simple rule: when this happens, do these things. The “when” is the trigger. The “do these things” are the actions. Each action uses a connector, which is a wrapper around a service such as Dataverse, Outlook, Teams or SharePoint.

Think of a doorbell. The doorbell is the trigger. Walking to the door, checking who it is and opening it are actions. A good doorbell rings only for real visitors, not for every passing car. A good trigger does the same: it fires only for the events that matter.

In PL-900 you built simple flows. At AB-410 level the exam expects you to recommend the right trigger, evaluate connectors against licensing and data policies, and configure actions precisely.

Why it matters

A badly chosen trigger wastes runs, hits service limits and creates confusing duplicates. Imagine a flow that emails the lab manager every time any Ticket column changes. A student edits a typo five times, and the manager gets five emails. With the right trigger settings, the flow would run once, only when Priority became High.

Connector choice matters too. Dataverse and HTTP are premium, so every user of the flow needs a suitable licence. Data policies (DLP) may block a flow that mixes a business connector with a personal one. Picking connectors early avoids a rebuild later.

How it works

1. Three kinds of trigger.

KindStarts whenExamples
AutomatedAn event happens in a serviceDataverse row changes, new email, new Forms response, SharePoint item created
InstantSomeone or something asks for itPower Apps (V2), Manually trigger a flow, a button in Teams, a Copilot Studio agent
ScheduledThe clock says soRecurrence every weekday at 07:00

2. The Dataverse trigger in depth. When a row is added, modified or deleted has several settings you must know:

  • Change type: Added, Modified, Deleted, or a combination.
  • Table name: the table to watch, such as Tickets.
  • Scope: whose rows count. User, Business unit, Parent: Child business unit, or Organization. For a shared help desk you usually want Organization.
  • Select columns: a comma-separated list of column logical names. A Modified event fires only when one of these columns changes.
  • Filter rows: an OData expression. Only rows that match start a run.
  • Run as: decides whose permissions later Dataverse actions use, such as the flow owner or the user who changed the row.
Select columns:  chd_priority,chd_status
Filter rows:     chd_priority eq 100000002 and _chd_category_value ne null

Choice columns store numbers, not labels. The number for High depends on your publisher’s choice value prefix, so always check the value in the column’s choice list. Lookups are filtered with the _name_value form shown above.

3. Trigger conditions. Every trigger has settings where you can add trigger conditions. These are expressions that must return true, or the run does not start at all. They are useful when the trigger has no filter of its own, for example an Outlook trigger that should only fire for subjects starting with “URGENT”.

@startsWith(triggerOutputs()?['body/subject'], 'URGENT')
Remember: a Condition action placed after the trigger still starts a run, uses an action and appears in run history. Filtering at the trigger stops the run from existing.

4. Evaluating connectors.

TypeExamplesThings to check
StandardOffice 365 Outlook, SharePoint, Teams, Forms, ApprovalsIncluded with Microsoft 365 use rights
PremiumDataverse, HTTP, SQL Server, many third-party servicesUsers need a premium licence (or the flow a per-flow plan)
CustomYour own REST API, such as a campus directoryBuilt from an OpenAPI definition; treated as premium

Also check data policies: connectors are grouped as Business, Non-business or Blocked, and one flow cannot mix Business and Non-business connectors. In a solution, flows use connection references so each environment can plug in its own connection.

5. Configuring actions. The common Dataverse actions are Add a new row, Update a row, Get a row by ID, List rows, Delete a row, Relate rows and Perform a bound action. List rows accepts Select columns, Filter rows, Sort by, Expand Query, Row count and even FetchXML. Always select only the columns you need; it makes flows faster and easier to read.

Data operation actions such as Compose, Select, Filter array and variables shape data between steps. Expressions format values:

Due: @{formatDateTime(triggerOutputs()?['body/chd_duedate'], 'dd MMM yyyy')}
Owner: @{coalesce(triggerOutputs()?['body/_ownerid_value'], 'Unassigned')}

Example: Campus Help Desk

The lab managers want one email when a ticket becomes High priority, including the category name.

  1. Create an automated flow inside the Campus Help Desk solution, so it travels with the other components.
  2. Trigger: Dataverse, change type Added or Modified, table Tickets, scope Organization.
  3. Select columns: chd_priority. Now edits to Title or Description do not start a run.
  4. Filter rows: chd_priority eq the High option value. Now Low and Medium changes are ignored.
  5. Action: Get a row by ID on Categories, using the trigger’s Category value. The trigger only gives the lookup ID, not the name.
  6. Action: Send an email (V2) to the lab managers group, with the title, category name and formatted due date.
  7. Check licensing: Dataverse is premium, but staff already use the premium model-driven app, so no extra licence decision is needed.
  8. Test by raising a ticket to High, then editing its title. Only the first edit creates a run.

Common mistakes

  • Filtering with a Condition action instead of the trigger. It works, but wastes runs and clutters history.
  • Comparing a choice column to its label text. Dataverse filters and conditions use the option’s numeric value.
  • Leaving Scope as User on a shared table, then wondering why the flow ignores other people’s tickets.
  • Forgetting that the flow owner’s connection is used by default, so actions run with that person’s permissions.
  • Building flows outside a solution, which makes them hard to move between Dev, Test and Production.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Only when column X changes” points to Select columns. “Only rows where…” points to Filter rows or a trigger condition.
  • “From a canvas app, pass values and return a result” points to Power Apps (V2) with Respond to a Power App or flow.
  • “Every night” or “on the first of the month” points to Recurrence plus List rows.
  • “Users without premium licences” or “blocked by policy” points to connector classification and data policies, not flow logic.

terms.definition: The event or request that starts a cloud flow; every flow has exactly one.
An OData expression on the Dataverse trigger or List rows action that limits which rows count, for example chd_status eq 1.
Trigger setting listing the columns whose change should fire a modified event; other column changes are ignored.
An expression in the trigger settings that must be true, or the run never starts.
A connector, such as Dataverse or HTTP, that needs a premium Power Automate or Power Apps licence.
A solution component that points a flow at a connection, so each environment can supply its own.

lessons.examTip: “Only when Priority changes” means Select columns on the Dataverse trigger. “Only for High tickets” means Filter rows or a trigger condition, not a Condition action after the trigger.

Select columns set to chd_status on the Dataverse trigger
A Recurrence trigger every five minutes
Scope set to User on the trigger

options: When a row is added, modified or deleted

options: A premium licence for the tester only

quiz.question: The flow should start only when a new ticket has Priority High and Category is set. You want to avoid wasted runs. What is the best approach?
options: Use a Condition as the first action and Terminate if false
Use a Do until loop to wait for the values
Use a Recurrence trigger that lists new tickets
Use Filter rows on the trigger, for example a priority test plus _chd_category_value ne null

lessons.title: Flow control, approvals and troubleshooting
lessons.summaryHtml:
Real processes branch, repeat, wait for people and sometimes fail. Cloud flows handle this with Condition and Switch for branching, Apply to each and Do until for loops, Scope to group actions, and Configure run after to decide what happens when something fails.

  • The Approvals connector sends requests to Outlook, Teams and the Approvals centre. Start and wait for an approval pauses the flow until the outcome is known.
  • Approval types decide whether everyone or the first responder decides, and whether answers are Approve/Reject or custom responses.
  • To troubleshoot, read the run history, inspect each action’s inputs and outputs, use Test with previous trigger data, and Resubmit failed runs after a fix.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A simple flow is a straight line. Real processes are not. Some tickets need approval and some do not. Some need the same step repeated for every item. Sometimes a service is down and a step fails. Flow control is how a flow makes decisions, repeats work, waits for people and recovers from errors.

Think of a railway line. Conditions and switches are the points that send a train down different tracks. Loops are the circle line that goes round until every station is served. Error handling is the emergency siding where a broken train is moved so it does not block everything else.

Why it matters

Help desks run on rules like “hardware over a certain value needs manager approval” and “chase the student every day until they reply”. If you cannot model branches, loops and waits, you end up with several half-flows and manual work. If you do not handle errors, a failed email silently leaves a ticket stuck, and nobody knows until a student complains.

AB-410 expects you to configure these patterns and to troubleshoot flows using run history, not guesswork.

How it works

1. Branching.

ControlUse whenHelp Desk example
ConditionA yes/no decision, with And/Or groupsIs Priority High and Due date within 2 days?
SwitchOne value with several possible casesCategory is Hardware, Software, Network or other
Parallel branchIndependent work that can happen at the same timeEmail the student and post to Teams together

2. Loops. Apply to each runs actions for every item in an array, such as rows returned by List rows. Its concurrency control setting lets iterations run in parallel, which is much faster but unsafe if iterations share a variable. Do until repeats until a condition is true, and always has a count limit and a timeout so it cannot run forever.

3. Scopes and run after. Every action has Configure run after. By default an action runs only if the previous one succeeded. You can also tick has failed, is skipped and has timed out. Combine this with Scope actions to build a try/catch pattern:

Scope "Try"      -> the normal steps
Scope "Catch"    -> run after Try: has failed, has timed out
   Compose       -> @{result('Try')}
   Send email    -> link to this run for the admin
   Terminate     -> Status: Failed

The result() expression returns the status and outputs of every action inside a scope, which helps you report what went wrong. Terminate ends the run with Succeeded, Failed or Cancelled, so monitoring shows the truth.

Actions that call services also have a retry policy in their settings, so short outages are retried automatically before the action is marked as failed.

4. Approvals. The Approvals connector sends requests that people answer in Outlook, Teams or the Approvals centre in Power Automate. Start and wait for an approval pauses the flow until the result comes back; Create an approval plus Wait for an approval lets you do work in between.

Approval typeOutcome decided by
Approve/Reject - Everyone must approveAll approvers must approve; any rejection rejects
Approve/Reject - First to respondThe first person who answers
Custom Responses - Wait for all responsesYour own options, such as Repair, Replace, Refuse; everyone answers
Custom Responses - Wait for one responseYour own options; the first answer wins

For sequential approvals (lab manager, then finance), place two approval actions one after the other, with a Condition between them. The outcome and each responder’s comments are available as dynamic content.

Watch out: a flow run has a maximum duration. Approvals that may wait for weeks need a reminder or escalation design, not an endless wait.

5. Testing and troubleshooting.

  • Flow checker in the designer lists errors and warnings before you save.
  • Test lets you run manually or reuse trigger data from a recent run, so you do not have to create a new ticket each time.
  • Run history shows recent runs with their status and duration. Open a run to see each action’s inputs, outputs and error message.
  • Resubmit runs a failed run again with its original trigger data after you fix the cause.
  • Common causes: expired or wrong connections, missing permissions for the run-as user, null values in expressions, and throttling when loops call a service too fast.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Hardware tickets need approval before a technician orders parts.

  1. A Power Apps (V2) flow receives TicketId from the staff app and uses Get a row by ID on Tickets.
  2. A Switch on the category name sends Hardware to an approval branch, Software straight to the software team, and the Default case to the general queue.
  3. In Hardware, Start and wait for an approval uses Approve/Reject - First to respond with two lab managers, so whoever is free decides.
  4. A Condition checks the Outcome. Approve sets Status to In progress. Reject closes the ticket and stores the approver’s comments.
  5. All of this sits in a Try scope. A Catch scope runs after Try has failed or timed out, emails the admin a link to the run with result('Try'), then Terminates as Failed.
  6. While testing, the maker passes a fake ID. Run history shows Get a row by ID failed with “not found”, Catch ran, and the email arrived. After the fix, the maker uses Resubmit.

Common mistakes

  • Nesting many Conditions when a single Switch on one value would be clearer.
  • Turning on concurrency in Apply to each while appending to a shared variable, which gives unpredictable results.
  • Catching errors but letting the run end as Succeeded, so nobody notices failures.
  • Choosing First to respond when policy says every manager must agree.
  • Recreating a flow instead of reading the failed action’s error in run history.

How the exam asks about it

  • “All must approve” versus “any one of” points to Everyone must approve versus First to respond. “Options other than approve and reject” points to custom responses.
  • “If a step fails, notify” points to configure run after and scopes. “Mark the run as failed” adds Terminate.
  • “Repeat until the student replies” points to Do until with a timeout. “For every row returned” points to Apply to each.
  • “Process the missed run again” points to Resubmit; “test without creating new data” points to Test with previous trigger data.

terms.definition: Branches on one value into several cases plus a default, cleaner than nested conditions.
Loops over an array; concurrency control can run iterations in parallel.
Repeats actions until a condition is true or its count or timeout limit is reached.
A container that groups actions so they can be collapsed and treated as one unit for run after.
Setting on an action that decides whether it runs after the previous one succeeded, failed, was skipped or timed out.

terms.term: Start and wait for an approval
terms.definition: Approvals action that sends a request and pauses the flow until the outcome is returned.

lessons.examTip: “Handle a failure and notify IT” means a Scope plus an action set to run after has failed or has timed out. “All managers must agree” means Approve/Reject - Everyone must approve.

steps: Download the exercise files. In the solution, create the instant flow Approve equipment ticket with the Power Apps (V2) trigger and a text input TicketId.

Build the outline at the top of approval-test-cases.md: Get a row by ID, a Switch with Hardware, Software and Default cases, the approval and the Condition, using the expressions in try-catch-expressions.txt.
Assign the approval to yourself and a second test user so you can answer it.

Move Get a row by ID and the Switch into a Scope named Try. Add a Scope named Catch, set its run after to has failed and has timed out on Try, and add the email and Terminate actions from try-catch-expressions.txt.
Copy the IDs of CHD-1026, CHD-1019, CHD-1018 and CHD-1025 from the address bar of each ticket in Help Desk Staff.
Run tests A1 to A6 from approval-test-cases.md, answering the approvals in Teams or Outlook.
For A5, open the run history and read the error and skipped actions as described in approval-test-cases.md, then do the clean-up.
check: A1: after you approve, CHD-1026 has Status In progress and the run shows Succeeded with Catch Skipped.
A2: after you reject, CHD-1019 has Status Closed and its description ends with “Rejected: Use a spare keyboard from lab 1”.
A3 and A4 send no approval request; A4’s Compose output reads “Routed to general queue”.
A5 sends you the Catch email with a working link to the run, and the run is marked Failed.

quiz.question: A laptop request needs agreement from both the lab manager and the finance officer, and the request is rejected if either rejects. Which approval type fits?
options: Custom responses - Wait for one response
Custom responses - Wait for all responses
quiz.explanation: Everyone must approve returns Approve only when every approver approves; one rejection gives a Reject outcome.

quiz.question: A flow updates many Dataverse rows inside Apply to each and runs slowly. Order does not matter and rows are independent. What should you change?
options: Turn on concurrency control on the Apply to each
Add a Delay inside the loop
Move the loop into a Switch
quiz.explanation: Concurrency control lets iterations run in parallel. It is safe only when iterations do not depend on each other or on a shared variable.

quiz.question: If any step that creates a ticket fails, a Teams message must go to the admin with details, and the flow run should still show as failed. What pattern should you use?
options: A Condition after each action checking for errors
Increase the retry policy to the maximum
A Do until loop around the steps
A Try Scope, a Catch Scope set to run after has failed, then Terminate with status Failed
quiz.explanation: Scopes with configure run after implement try/catch. Terminate with Failed keeps the run marked as failed so monitoring still sees it.

quiz.question: A scheduled flow failed last night because a connection expired. You fixed the connection. What is the quickest way to process the same trigger again?
options: Resubmit the failed run from the run history
Change the Recurrence to run every minute
quiz.explanation: Resubmit reruns the flow with the original trigger data, so the missed work is done without waiting for the next schedule.

lessons.title: AI Hub prompts
lessons.summaryHtml:
A prompt (built with prompt builder, found under AI hub > Prompts in Power Apps and Power Automate) is a reusable generative AI tool. You write instructions, add inputs that apps and flows fill in at run time, and optionally ground it with knowledge such as Dataverse data.

  • Start from Build your own prompt or a prompt template from the prompt library (tasks such as summarize, classify, extract, create).
  • Inputs are Text or Image or document. Each input needs a sample value so you can Test.
  • Settings include the model, temperature (0 to 1, default 0), record retrieval, include links in the response, code interpreter and content moderation level.
  • Output can be Text or JSON. JSON gives flows and apps typed properties, so no Parse JSON step is needed.
  • Consume a prompt in a flow with Run a prompt, and in a canvas app by adding it as data and calling .Predict().
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A prompt in Power Platform is a saved set of instructions for a generative AI model, with blanks that your apps and flows fill in. You build it once in prompt builder and reuse it everywhere: in canvas apps, in cloud flows and in Copilot Studio agents.

Think of a well-written form letter with gaps: “Dear ___, your ticket about ___ is ___.” The prompt is the letter and its instructions. The inputs are the gaps. The model writes the rest. Because the prompt is a proper Power Platform component, it lives in solutions and moves between environments like any other part of your app.

In Power Apps and Power Automate you find prompts under AI hub > Prompts. The same prompt builder is also used in Copilot Studio, where a prompt becomes a tool an agent can call.

Why it matters

Many business tasks are language tasks: summarise a long description, classify a request, extract a date from an email, draft a reply. Before prompts, each needed a trained model or custom code. Now a maker writes clear instructions, tests them with sample data and plugs the prompt into a flow.

The exam focuses on doing this well: choosing templates, adding inputs, grounding with knowledge, tuning settings, returning structured JSON and consuming the prompt correctly in apps and flows.

How it works

1. Starting point. In AI hub > Prompts you can choose Build your own prompt (blank) or Start from a prompt template. The prompt library holds predesigned templates grouped by job type (for example Customer service, IT, HR) and by task (Analyze, Classify, Create, Extract, Summarize). A template gives you tested wording and example inputs that you then adapt.

2. Instructions. Good instructions say what to do and give context: the role, the task, the rules, and the exact shape of the answer. Short, specific instructions beat long, vague ones.

3. Inputs. Inputs are named placeholders inserted into the instructions. There are two kinds:

Input typeWhat it carriesHelp Desk use
TextAny string passed at run timeThe ticket description
Image or documentA file such as a photo or PDFA photo of a broken projector

Each input needs a sample value. Prompt builder uses sample values when you select Test, so you see a real response before saving.

4. Knowledge. You can ground a prompt with knowledge, such as rows from a Dataverse table. You add the table, pick the columns to include and can filter rows, including by an input value. The model then answers using your real data instead of guessing. This is how you stop a classifier inventing categories that do not exist.

5. Settings. Open the three dots (…) > Settings in prompt builder. Also choose the model at the top.

SettingWhat it does
ModelWhich generative model runs the prompt. A small, fast model is the default; larger general and deep reasoning models cost more per run. Some models are managed by Microsoft; others are external.
Temperature0 to 1, default 0. Low gives predictable output; high gives more varied, creative output.
Record retrievalHow many records are retrieved from knowledge sources.
Include links in the responseAdds link citations to the retrieved records.
Enable code interpreterLets the model generate and run code, for example to calculate or process files.
Content moderation levelLow to High, default Moderate; available for managed models only.

The list of available models changes often, so check it in prompt builder rather than memorising names.

6. Output: Text or JSON. By default the output is Text. Choose JSON in the top-right corner of prompt builder for structured data. The format is Auto detected from your latest test until you edit the JSON example, which makes it Custom (select Save custom to keep it). When you save the prompt, the format is locked, so apps and flows always get the same shape.

7. Consuming the prompt.

  • Cloud flow: the AI Builder action Run a prompt. Choose the prompt and fill the inputs with dynamic content. A Text prompt gives a Text output; a JSON prompt gives typed properties, so you do not need Parse JSON.
  • Canvas app: select Data > Add data, add the prompt, then call it with .Predict() from a button and store the result.
  • Copilot Studio: add the prompt as a tool on an agent or call it from a topic.
// Button OnSelect
Set(varSummary, 'Summarize ticket'.Predict(txtDescription.Text));
// Label Text
varSummary.text
Remember: each prompt run consumes AI capacity. Call prompts from a deliberate action, such as a button or a trigger with good filters, not on every keystroke.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The team wants every new ticket classified automatically.

  1. In AI hub > Prompts, the maker starts from a Classify template and renames it “Classify ticket”.
  2. Instruction: “You are a campus IT help desk triage assistant. Read the ticket description. Choose exactly one category from the knowledge provided and one priority: Low, Medium or High. High means teaching or exams are blocked today. Give a one-sentence reason.”
  3. Input: Text, named TicketDescription, sample “Projector in B12 shows no signal and my lecture starts in an hour”.
  4. Knowledge: Dataverse table Categories, with name and description columns.
  5. Settings: temperature 0, because triage must be consistent. Default model, since the task is simple.
  6. Output: JSON. After testing, the detected format has category, priority and reason. The maker saves the prompt.
  7. A Dataverse-triggered flow on new tickets calls Run a prompt, then uses the typed priority and category values to update the row. A List rows action finds the Category row by name to set the lookup.

Common mistakes

  • Returning Text and parsing it with string functions, when JSON output gives typed fields.
  • Raising temperature to “make it smarter”. Temperature controls variety, not accuracy.
  • Writing a long list of categories into the instruction instead of grounding with the Categories table, which then goes stale.
  • Testing without realistic sample values, so the auto-detected JSON format misses fields.
  • Calling the prompt from OnChange in a canvas app, running it many times per edit.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Structured values for later actions” points to JSON output. “No Parse JSON” confirms it.
  • “Use our own data” or “only existing values” points to adding Dataverse knowledge.
  • “Consistent, repeatable results” points to low temperature. “Citations” points to include links in the response.
  • “In a flow” points to Run a prompt; “in a canvas app” points to adding the prompt as data and calling Predict.

terms.definition: The designer where you write a prompt’s instructions, inputs, knowledge, settings and output format, then test and save it.

lessons.title: AI models in apps and flows
lessons.summaryHtml:
Besides prompts, AI hub gives you AI models (the AI Builder models). Prebuilt models are ready to use: sentiment analysis, key phrase extraction, language detection, text translation, entity extraction, category classification, text recognition, invoice, receipt, ID and business card processing. Custom models are trained on your own data: document processing, object detection, prediction, and custom category classification and entity extraction.

  • In a canvas app, add the model under Add data > AI models and call ModelName.Predict(…), usually from a button, storing the result in a variable.
  • In a cloud flow, use the AI Builder connector: a model-specific action such as Analyze positive or negative sentiment or Process documents, or the generic Predict action.
  • Custom models must be trained and published before apps and flows can use them.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A prompt is flexible: you describe any task in words. An AI model in AI hub is a specialist: it does one kind of job, such as reading receipts or measuring sentiment, and returns the same structured result every time. These are the AI Builder models.

Think of tools in a workshop. A prompt is a multi-tool that can do many things reasonably well. A model is a dedicated tool, like a torque wrench, built for one job with measurable precision. You pick the tool that fits the task.

Why it matters

Some tasks need reliable, repeatable structure: the total on an invoice, the fields on a form, the probability that feedback is negative. Specialist models return fixed fields and confidence scores, which are easy to test, filter and audit. For your own documents or historical data, a custom model learns your patterns.

AB-410 asks you to choose between prebuilt and custom models and to consume them in canvas apps and cloud flows.

How it works

1. Prebuilt and custom.

DataPrebuilt (no training)Custom (you train)
DocumentsInvoice processing, receipt processing, ID reader, business card reader, text recognition, contract processingDocument processing (your own layouts)
TextSentiment analysis, key phrase extraction, language detection, text translation, entity extraction, category classificationCategory classification, entity extraction
Structured dataNonePrediction (from historical Dataverse rows)
ImagesText recognitionObject detection

The prebuilt category classification model uses fixed customer-feedback categories (such as Issues, Compliment and Price & Billing). If you need your own categories, use a custom model or a prompt grounded with your Categories table.

2. Custom model lifecycle. You create the model in AI hub, provide data (sample documents with labelled fields, tagged images, or a Dataverse table with a historical outcome column), train it, review its performance score, then publish it. Only published models can be used in apps and flows. When your data changes, you retrain and publish a new version.

3. Using a model in a canvas app. Select Data > Add data > AI models and pick the model. You then call it with Predict. The argument names depend on the model type.

// Button OnSelect
Set(varSentiment, 'Sentiment analysis'.Predict(txtFeedback.Text));
Set(varLang, 'Language detection'.Predict(txtFeedback.Text).Language);
// Custom object detection on a captured image
Set(varObjects, 'Lab equipment detector'.Predict(Camera1.Photo))

Microsoft recommends calling Predict from a single action such as a button’s OnSelect, not OnChange, and saving the result in a variable to reuse. Some model types also have ready-made AI Builder controls you can insert on a screen, such as the business card reader.

4. Using a model in a cloud flow. The AI Builder connector offers model-specific actions and a generic one:

ActionUse for
Analyze positive or negative sentimentPrebuilt sentiment; returns overall sentiment and probabilities
Process documentsCustom document processing model; pass the file and document type, get fields, tables and confidence
Actions for invoices, receipts, text recognition and othersThe matching prebuilt model
PredictAny published model, including a model ID passed dynamically for document processing

Outputs come back as dynamic content. Use the confidence score in a Condition so low-confidence results go to a person for review instead of straight into Dataverse.

5. Prompt or model?

NeedBetter fit
Standard task with a fixed output, such as sentiment or receiptsPrebuilt model
Your own form layouts, image objects or historical outcomesCustom model
Free-form instructions, summaries, drafts, flexible classificationPrompt
Remember: AI usage is metered. Microsoft is moving AI Builder features from AI Builder credits to Copilot Credits, so capacity planning belongs in your design, whichever option you choose.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Students leave free-text feedback when a ticket is closed. A flow triggers on Tickets with Select columns set to the feedback column.
  2. It calls Analyze positive or negative sentiment with the feedback and Language en.
  3. A Condition checks Probability overall text is negative. Above 0.7, it writes Negative to a sentiment column and emails the team lead. Otherwise it stores the overall sentiment.
  4. Facilities send repair quotes as PDFs in one fixed supplier layout. The team trains a document processing model on sample quotes, labelling quote number, total and line items, then publishes it.
  5. A second flow runs when a quote arrives by email, calls Process documents, and adds the total to the ticket. If the total’s confidence is low, it starts an approval instead of writing the value.
  6. In the student canvas app, a button calls 'Key phrase extraction'.Predict(txtDescription.Text) and shows the phrases, so students can check their description is clear before submitting.

Common mistakes

  • Training a custom model for a job a prebuilt model already does, such as sentiment.
  • Expecting the prebuilt category classification model to use your own categories.
  • Forgetting to publish a trained model, then not finding it in the app or flow.
  • Ignoring confidence scores and writing every extracted value straight into Dataverse.
  • Calling Predict in OnChange or in a control’s property, which runs it far more often than needed.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Common task, no training data” points to a prebuilt model. “Our own layout” points to custom document processing.
  • “Historical rows and a yes/no outcome” points to a prediction model. “Find items in photos” points to object detection.
  • “In a canvas app” points to Add data > AI models and Predict from a button. “Choose the model at run time” points to the Predict action with a dynamic model ID.
  • “Low confidence must be reviewed” points to a Condition on the confidence score, often with an approval.
