lessons.title: Business rules, process flows and calculated columns
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dataverse gives you no-code places to put logic close to the data. Business rules set values, show errors, make columns required, lock or hide them. Business process flows (BPFs) guide users through stages and steps. Formula, calculated and rollup columns compute values automatically.

  • A business rule with scope Entity (table) runs on the server and on all forms; a form scope runs only in the forms.
  • A formula column uses Power Fx and is calculated when the row is read. Calculated columns are the older equivalent.
  • A rollup column aggregates related rows (count, sum, min, max, average) and is recalculated by a system job, not instantly.
  • Cloud flows handle anything that needs other systems, waits or notifications. Canvas app Power Fx handles logic that only matters in one app’s screens.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Not all logic needs a flow or code. Dataverse has built-in, no-code places to put rules right next to the data: business rules, business process flows and computed columns (formula, calculated and rollup).

Think of a well-run office. Business rules are the form that will not let you submit without a date. A business process flow is the checklist on the wall that shows which stage a job is at. A formula column is the clock that always shows the current time. A rollup column is the tally board that someone updates regularly.

Why it matters

Logic in the wrong place causes trouble. A rule written only in a canvas app is skipped when staff edit data in the model-driven app. A nightly flow that calculates “days open” is wrong for most of the day. A cloud flow used for simple validation adds delay and uses runs. The exam tests whether you can put each rule in the simplest place that still applies everywhere it must.

How it works

1. Business rules. You build them in a visual designer on a table. A rule has conditions (if, with And/Or) and actions:

  • Set column value, clear column value, set default value.
  • Set business required (required, recommended, not required).
  • Show error message on a column.
  • Lock or unlock a column; show or hide a column.
  • Show a recommendation (forms only).
ScopeRuns
Entity (the table)On the server and on all model-driven forms, so imports, flows and API updates are covered for server-side actions
All formsOnly in model-driven forms of that table
A specific formOnly in that form

Show/hide, lock and recommendation actions only make sense on forms, so they have no effect at server level. Because Entity-scope rules run on the server, their server-side actions also apply when a canvas app or a flow saves to Dataverse.

2. Business process flows. A BPF guides users through stages, each with data steps (columns to fill). It appears as a bar at the top of model-driven forms.

  • Steps can be required, which blocks moving to the next stage until they are filled.
  • Stages can branch with conditions, and a BPF can span more than one related table.
  • Each BPF is stored as its own Dataverse table, so you can report on which stage each ticket is in and how long it stayed there.
  • A stage can trigger actions or flows, and security roles control who can use each BPF.

3. Computed columns.

Column typeHow it calculatesWhen the value updates
Formula columnPower Fx, from the same row and related rowsWhen the row is retrieved, so always current
Calculated columnOlder designer with conditions and actionsWhen retrieved; Microsoft now recommends formula columns
Rollup columnCount, sum, min, max or average of related child rows, with optional filtersBy a scheduled system job, or on demand with refresh
 
// Formula column chd_daysopen on Ticket (Whole number)
DateDiff('Created On', UTCNow(), TimeUnit.Days)

Computed columns are read-only. You cannot type into them, and they are ideal for views, charts and sorting.

4. Choosing the right place.

NeedPlace
Validate, default or require values on a tableBusiness rule
Value derived from the same row, always currentFormula column
Aggregate of related rowsRollup column
Guided, staged process for usersBusiness process flow
Other systems, notifications, waits, approvals, schedulesCloud flow
Behaviour of one canvas app’s screensPower Fx in the canvas app
Complex server logic that must be synchronousPlug-in (developer, covered in AB-400)
Remember: the closer the logic sits to the data, the more places it applies. Table-level logic (Entity-scope rules, formula and rollup columns) covers every app and integration.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Business rule on Ticket, scope Entity: if Priority equals High and Due date does not contain data, show an error on Due date. A flow that creates a High ticket without a due date now fails with that message, just like the form.
  2. Business rule, scope All forms: if Status equals Closed, lock the Description column so staff cannot rewrite history.
  3. Formula column chd_daysopen on Ticket shows days since creation. Staff sort the Active Tickets view by it.
  4. Rollup column chd_opentickets on Category counts related Tickets where Status is Open. The Categories view shows workload per team, refreshed by the system job.
  5. Business process flow “Ticket lifecycle”: New (Category, Priority), Assigned (Owner), Resolved (Resolution, required), Closed (Closed on). Staff cannot move to Closed without a resolution.
  6. Emailing the student at closure stays in a cloud flow, because it uses Outlook.

Common mistakes

  • Using All forms scope for a rule that must also apply to imports and flows. Only Entity scope runs on the server.
  • Expecting rollup columns to update instantly after a child row changes.
  • Using a nightly flow to write values that a formula column can compute at read time.
  • Putting validation only in a canvas app, so the model-driven app and integrations skip it.
  • Treating a BPF as automation. It guides people; it does not send emails or call services by itself.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Without code, on every form and for imported data” points to a business rule with Entity scope.
  • “Total, count or average of related records” points to a rollup column; “acceptable delay” confirms it.
  • “Always up to date when viewed” or “Power Fx column” points to a formula column.
  • “Stages”, “guide users” or “cannot move on until…” points to a business process flow.

terms.definition: No-code logic on a table: set or clear values, show error messages, set requirement, lock or show/hide columns.
Where a rule runs: Entity (table-level, server and forms), All forms, or one specific form.
A guided sequence of stages and data steps shown at the top of model-driven forms.
A Power Fx column calculated at read time from values in the same or related rows.
A column that aggregates related child rows, refreshed by a scheduled system job or on demand.

lessons.examTip: “Must also apply when data is imported or changed by a flow” points to a business rule with Entity scope. “Total of related rows” points to a rollup column. “Guide the user through stages” points to a business process flow.

quiz.question: Tickets are also created by a flow and by data import. Every High ticket must have a Due date no matter how it is created. Which no-code option works everywhere?
options: Business rule with scope All forms
quiz.explanation: Entity scope runs the rule on the server as well as on forms, so it applies to imports and flows. Form scopes run only when a form is open.

quiz.question: Each Category form must show how many open tickets it has. A delay before the number updates is acceptable. Which column type fits?

quiz.explanation: A BPF shows stages at the top of the form, with data steps that can be required before moving to the next stage.

quiz.question: A column must show the number of days a ticket has been open, always current when the row is viewed, without a scheduled job. Which option is best?
options: Recurrence flow updating every row nightly
quiz.explanation: Formula columns are calculated when the row is retrieved, so the value is current. A nightly flow would be stale during the day and would use extra runs.
